Title: Literature Review: Emerging Innovation Frontiers in Healthcare and Their Transformative Impact on Sustainability—Implications for Adoption Barriers and Leadership-Governance Dynamics

Introduction and Conceptual Framing
Healthcare systems worldwide are converging on an “innovation frontier” that spans digital technologies, artificial intelligence, value-based and population health models, integrated care platforms, and workforce and governance redesigns. Sustainability in this context is multidimensional: environmental (carbon, waste, energy), social (equity, patient experience, workforce well-being), and economic (cost efficiency, resilience). A mixed-method approach is needed because, while digitalization can deliver measurable gains in emissions, access, and cost, its system-wide sustainability depends on organizational readiness, governance quality, and adaptive decision-making that reconcile technical promise with human, workflow, and policy realities. <cite id="780532a3-0">Digitalization of care, including telemedicine and AI, can reduce sectoral environmental impacts yet introduces energy and e-waste burdens, demanding lifecycle-aware strategies aligned with planetary health goals</cite> <cite id="780532a3-3">Digital health impact assessments often emphasize experience and population health but underweight environmental and equity dimensions within value-based frameworks, signaling a need for holistic evaluation</cite>.

Emerging Innovation Frontiers in Healthcare
Emerging frontiers are coalescing around three pillars: (1) digitally enabled, data-driven care; (2) integrated and population-based delivery; and (3) adaptive governance and workforce models. <cite id="780532a3-0">Scoping across 58 studies shows telemedicine as the dominant digital vector for sustainability impacts, with most work quantifying transport emissions avoided and many reporting concurrent gains in patient experience, time efficiency, and cost</cite> <cite id="780532a3-3">A systematic mapping of digital health impact studies found that while experience of care and population health are frequently assessed, environmental and equity outcomes remain marginal, reinforcing the need to balance technical and social aims</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-3">A Holistic Impact Framework integrating underrepresented social and environmental dimensions complements the Triple Aim and provides a planning scaffold for mixed-method evaluations</cite>.

Digital Technologies and Sustainable Healthcare: Environmental, Social, and Economic Effects
Environmental effects
Digitalization can cut greenhouse gas emissions by displacing travel and consolidating care. <cite id="780532a3-0">Across 58 studies, 91% focused on telemedicine; 97% quantified transport-related emissions reductions, with total avoided emissions estimated at approximately 830 million kg CO2</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-0">However, only 12% evaluated full life cycle impacts, underscoring the risk that energy-intensive infrastructure and device manufacturing erode environmental benefits</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-1">Digital tools may reduce some environmental footprints but can also increase energy use through rebound effects and by expanding digital infrastructures; adoption without behavioral or systemic change can leave environmental outcomes unchanged</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-2">Health systems’ dual roles as climate responders and drivers mandate aligning digitalization with environmental goals and policy to avoid contradictions between growth and sustainability</cite>.

Social effects
Digital care often improves patient-centered experience and care coordination. <cite id="780532a3-0">A majority of studies emphasized higher satisfaction, time efficiency, and convenience, alongside reduced burden for caregivers</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-3">Digital health assessments increasingly capture experience-of-care and population health while offering tools to embed equity into design, yet environmental and transparency dimensions remain limited</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Organizational readiness and change management mediate whether digital tools translate into daily practice; leadership that shapes culture and involvement reduces resistance among older, less engaged staff and improves sustained use</cite>.

Economic effects
Cost reductions and efficiency gains are common but contingent on integration quality. <cite id="780532a3-0">Economic analyses often highlight lower costs and resource optimization from digitalization</cite> <cite id="780532a3-4">Electronic health records reduce errors and costs relative to paper-based systems and telemedicine extends access and cost savings in underserved areas when paired with supportive policies and management</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-1">System-wide adoption is more likely when interoperability, data governance, workforce capacity, and multi-stakeholder engagement are co-developed with policy frameworks; sustained enhancement depends on adaptive strategies aligned to local capacity</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Leadership that combines strategic vision, digital literacy, and participative inclusion fosters organizational climate for innovation, aligning technological, cultural, and human factors to sustain economic and quality gains</cite>.

Hidden Catalysts and Bottlenecks: Barriers to Sustainable Adoption
Organizational and workflow barriers
<cite id="320e7d7f-0">Even with leadership commitment, digital tools can feel burdensome when excluded from design or perceived as useless; generational and role-fit mismatches reduce engagement and sustain low utilization</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Older staff frequently perceive EHRs as irrelevant to their roles, signaling gaps in user involvement and change management that impede behavioral adoption despite technological availability</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Across settings, interoperability deficits, limited digital literacy, resistance to change, and unclear governance structures undermine consistent, safe integration of digital systems</cite>.

Governance, policy, and ecosystem barriers
<cite id="320e7d7f-1">Integrated policy frameworks with proactive organizational readiness improve interoperability, data governance, and adoption, while adaptive strategies tailored to resource constraints support sustainable system enhancement</cite>. <cite id="451d5c01-4">Complexity-compatible policy design (e.g., Ontario’s Health Links) that emphasizes local experimentation and learning succeeds when leadership, readiness, relationship-building, role clarity, communication, and resources are in place; yet tensions between flexibility and standardization can stall scaling, and desirable developments often remain piecemeal without vertical integration of learning</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-1">Energy- and resource-intensive infrastructures and rebound effects can erode environmental benefits if governance fails to manage growth in digital demand alongside health outcomes</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Leadership that integrates digital, cultural, and human domains and clarifies ethical governance, safety, and regulatory compliance is pivotal; absent leadership, digital change can amplify alert fatigue, workload, and safety risks and widen inequities</cite>.

Equity and inclusion
<cite id="780532a3-3">Digital health frameworks increasingly embed equity into the Sextuple Aim, yet only a minority of studies assess environmental and equity outcomes jointly, revealing gaps in measuring distributional impacts</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Workforce capacity, inclusive decision-making, and ethical governance mitigate inequities in access and family engagement during digital NICU transformation, with leadership competencies shaping outcomes</cite>.

Leadership Mindsets, Governance Styles, and Adaptive Decision-Making as Catalysts or Bottlenecks
Complex adaptive systems lens
Healthcare is a complex adaptive system (CAS): interdependent actors, evolving interactions, and emergent outcomes make standard control-based strategies brittle. <cite id="451d5c01-0">Healthcare’s CAS properties create unpredictability in implementation; traditional change management may be ill-suited, requiring leaders to embrace uncertainty, minimize rigid specifications, and use enabling, entrepreneurial, and operational leadership roles to create adaptive space</cite> <cite id="451d5c01-1">Outcomes emerge from interdependent agent interactions; resilient healthcare emphasizes flexibility, feedback, and local decision-making over rigid workflows, with leadership mindsets evolving through engagement with unpredictable clinical work</cite>.

Adaptive and distributed leadership
<cite id="451d5c01-3">Adaptive leadership mobilizes people to confront challenges, experiment with solutions, and build resilience in the face of climate, disease, and resource uncertainty; integrating adaptive, servant, and transformational models fosters inclusivity and long-term sustainability</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-0">Planetary Health-aligned digitalization demands leadership capable of balancing emission reductions with infrastructure growth and governance that embeds sustainability into strategy</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-2">Transformational, participative, and digital leadership combined can overcome adoption barriers by aligning strategic vision, inclusion, and technical expertise to create climates conducive to innovation and sustained improvement</cite>.

Governance as a hidden bottleneck
<cite id="451d5c01-4">Even in “low rules” complexity-compatible designs, leadership, readiness, relationship-building, role clarity, communication, and resources are decisive; failures in vertical information flow leave scaling efforts fragmented and ad hoc</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Leadership influences acceptance indirectly by shaping culture and expectations; when leadership is weak or exclusionary, adoption falters despite available technology</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Poorly governed digital change can increase workload and safety risks and widen inequities; leadership competencies in ethics, safety, and stakeholder coordination become first-order determinants of sustainable outcomes</cite>.

Governance as a catalyst for system-wide change
<cite id="451d5c01-0">Enabling leadership that fosters learning, creativity, and adaptability supports system function as a CAS and sustains innovation diffusion</cite> <cite id="451d5c01-1">Resilient healthcare emphasizes continuous feedback and local decision-making to anticipate and recover from disruptions, aligning governance with adaptive capacity</cite>. <cite id="451d5c01-2">Sustainable improvement requires integrated pathways: patient-centered and value-based care, operational efficiency, digital health, workforce development, and supportive policy frameworks; governance that aligns incentives and embeds accountability is indispensable for scaling innovations</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-1">Integrated, adaptive policy combined with organizational readiness, workforce capacity building, and multi-sector engagement creates durable system change</cite>.

Case evidence: Integrated care and digital NICU
<cite id="451d5c01-4">Ontario’s Health Links illustrates how complexity-compatible policy can stimulate local experimentation and learning, but only where leadership balances flexibility and consistency and coordinates across levels; absent such governance, improvements remain piecemeal</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-3">In neonatal care, nursing-led digital transformation improves outcomes only when leadership models, workflow integration, and ethical governance address alert fatigue, workload, and family engagement; facilitators and barriers map directly to leadership competencies and governance quality</cite>.

Implications for Mixed-Methods Research and Practice
Designing for sustainability
<cite id="780532a3-0">Planetary Health provides a framework to align digitalization with climate mitigation, emphasizing that benefits depend on lifecycle-aware strategies and governance that embed environmental accountability</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-3">The Sextuple Aim plus a Holistic Impact Framework can integrate experience, population health, costs, team well-being, equity, and environmental impacts into coherent decision-making</cite>.

Assessing and accelerating adoption
<cite id="320e7d7f-0">Organizational readiness, sustained capacity building, and inclusive design reduce resistance and improve sustained use; leadership that shapes culture and expectations can be qualitatively predictive of adoption even when direct metrics are weak</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-1">Policy-innovation plus organizational transformation with interoperability, data governance, workforce capacity, and stakeholder engagement yields higher sustainability and resilience of digital systems</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Leadership integrating vision, digital literacy, participative inclusion, and adaptive decision-making aligns human, workflow, and policy domains to avoid rebound and inequity traps</cite>.

Governance diagnostics and adaptive evaluation
<cite id="451d5c01-4">Complexity-compatible governance should monitor both local learning dynamics and vertical translation of lessons; balancing flexibility and consistency under capable leadership prevents patchy diffusion and blocked scaling</cite>. <cite id="451d5c01-1">Adopting resilient-healthcare principles—continuous feedback loops, local decision-making, and workarounds-as-data—supports adaptive evaluation that distinguishes true system change from superficial workflow digitization</cite>.

Proposed Contributions of the Mixed-Methods Study
- Mapping emerging frontiers: triangulate environmental, social, and economic outcomes across digital innovations using VAH- and VBHC-aligned metrics and planetary health framing. <cite id="780532a3-0">Planetary Health-aligned digitalization demands lifecycle-aware strategies and actionable governance</cite> <cite id="780532a3-3">The Sextuple Aim provides a scaffold to quantify experience, population health, and equity alongside environmental metrics</cite>.
- Barriers landscape and governance interventions: combine quantitative indicators (interoperability, safety incidents, emissions intensity) with qualitative sensemaking (leadership narratives, workflow ethnography, stakeholder forums) to explain where governance bottlenecks or hidden cultural barriers stall adoption. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Leadership and culture mediate technology-to-practice translation</cite> <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Governance quality shapes safety, workload, and equity risks in digital transformation</cite>.
- Leadership and system change: evaluate adaptive leadership competencies, distributed decision-making, and coalition governance against measures of diffusion, resilience, and equity of impact. <cite id="451d5c01-0">CAS-informed leadership roles enable adaptive space and learning</cite> <cite id="451d5c01-3">Adaptive leadership mobilizes experimentation and resilience to sustainability challenges</cite>.

Conclusions and Research Agenda
Digital technologies are reshaping healthcare’s environmental, social, and economic footprints, but their sustainability is contingent on governance that integrates lifecycle impacts, equity, and adaptive capacity. <cite id="780532a3-0">Telemedicine can avoid hundreds of thousands of metric tons of CO2 while improving experience and costs, yet benefits depend on lifecycle analyses and governance that constrains rebound and infrastructure lock-in</cite> <cite id="780532a3-1">Digitalization may also increase energy and resource use if adoption is not matched by systemic and behavioral change</cite>. Organizational readiness, interoperability, workforce capacity, and ethical governance are necessary to translate innovation into durable, equitable improvements. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Leadership shapes culture and inclusion, which often determine whether digital tools are adopted and sustained</cite> <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Leadership that fuses vision, digital acumen, and participative decision-making aligns human and technical systems to avoid safety and equity pitfalls</cite>. At the system level, complexity-compatible governance, resilient decision-making, and vertical integration of learning are the hidden levers of sustainable transformation. <cite id="451d5c01-4">Balancing local experimentation with consistent policy guidance under capable leadership prevents piecemeal diffusion and accelerates system-wide change</cite>. Future work should expand lifecycle and socio-environmental assessments, develop governance capacity-building roadmaps, and embed adaptive evaluation into digital health portfolios to ensure that emerging frontiers deliver long-term sustainability and equitable value. <cite id="780532a3-0">Actionable strategies for sustainable digitalization must move beyond telemedicine alone and embed lifecycle analyses and climate-aligned governance</cite> <cite id="780532a3-2">Aligning digital innovation with environmental goals requires integrated organizational and policy responses</cite> <cite id="451d5c01-2">Sustainable healthcare excellence emerges from integrated pathways that align patient-centered care, operational efficiency, digital innovation, workforce development, and policy frameworks</cite>.

Title: Aligning With the Goals of the Planetary Health Concept Regarding Ecological Sustainability and Digital Health: Scoping Review
Snippet: Background Climate change, driven by greenhouse gas emissions, threatens human health and biodiversity. While the digitalization of health care, including telemedicine and artificial intelligence, offers sustainability benefits, it also raises concerns about energy use and electronic waste. Balancing these factors is key to a sustainable health care future. Objective The objective of this review was to examine the extent to which digitalization in the health care sector influences environmental sustainability. Specifically, it aimed to assess how digitalization can contribute to reducing the health care sector’s impact on global climate change. From these findings, conclusions were drawn regarding the extent to which digitalization aligns with the objectives of the Planetary Health movement and how these 2 movements may mutually reinforce each other. Methods A scoping review guided by the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines using databases such as PubMed and Scopus was conducted, and 58 quantitative studies from 2009 to 2024 were analyzed for environmental, social, and economic outcomes aligned with Planetary Health goals. Results This review analyzed 58 studies on the environmental impact of digitalization in health care primarily focusing on telemedicine, which was examined in 91% (53/58) of the studies. Most studies (56/58, 97%) quantified transport-related emissions avoided through digitalization, with some also assessing emissions from health care facilities, medical equipment, and energy consumption. Findings indicated that telemedicine significantly reduces carbon dioxide emissions, with total avoided emissions amounting to approximately 830 million kg. A substantial proportion of the studies (36/58, 62%) focused on social aspects, highlighting factors such as patient satisfaction, time efficiency, and overall convenience. In addition, economic considerations were analyzed in 48% (28/58) of the studies, emphasizing cost reductions and resource optimization. However, only 12% (7/58) of the studies evaluated the full life cycle impact of digital technologies, highlighting the need for further research on their long-term environmental sustainability. Conclusions This review calls for further research beyond telemedicine, advocating for life cycle analyses and actionable strategies for a sustainable digitalization in health care systems. The Planetary Health framework is highlighted as a guide for ensuring sustainable digital transformation in health care.
</snippet>

Title: Why digital innovation may not alleviate healthcare’s environmental impacts
Snippet: Healthcare is becoming increasingly digitalised through innovations in information and communication technologies, including monitoring devices, streaming, data storage, and increasingly through advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) (1). Advocates enthuse that this digitalisation will improve key aspects of healthcare delivery, including enhanced safety, accessibility, quality of care, effectiveness, and efficiency (2). Others debate whether these promises can be met because of complex social, cultural, economic, and political implementation challenges (3). More recently, digital innovation has been promised as a means to reduce the environmental impacts associated with healthcare delivery (4). Healthcare systems contribute to approximately 5.5% of a country's total greenhouse gas emissions, with this figure often being higher in high income countries (HICs) (5). In this paper we argue that digitalisation could indeed reduce environmental impacts, but that it is also possible that these technologies might be implemented in ways that do not lead to reductions, and indeed may increase resource use with little change to health outcomes. We discuss current evidence that shows how digital innovation could reduce the environmental impacts of healthcare. Then we focus on two aspects that need to be considered when developing plans for a digitally enabled and environmentally sustainable healthcare system, namely the growing energy-and resource-intensive digital infrastructures required, and the paradoxical increase in energy use associated with the introduction of energy-saving technologies-the so called "rebound effect". Our perspective predominantly reflects HIC health systems, though our arguments are relevant globally, and we also draw on and discuss low and middle income country (LMIC) contexts.

Title: Evaluating holistic socio-environmental impact of digital health: scoping review of decision-making frameworks
Snippet: The 2030 Agenda highlights the transformative role of digital technologies in advancing human progress, reducing inequalities and promoting sustainable knowledge societies. Digital Health (DH) enhances healthcare effectiveness, resilience and equity, while addressing environmental and climate challenges. To fill a literature gap, we conducted a scoping review of methodologies for DH impact assessment, focusing on social and environmental dimensions aligned with the six aims of Value-Based Health Care (VBHC).
 
 
 
 The review followed JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane searches (2014–2024, English) retrieved studies addressing at least three domains of the Sextuple Aim: Experience of Care, Population Health, Reduced Cost, Care Team Well-Being, Health Equity, and Environmental Impact.
 
 
 
 From 8,243 records, 53 studies met criteria. None addressed all six aims. Experience of Care (98.11%) and Population Health (94.34%) dominated assessments, whereas Environmental Impact appeared in 11.32%. Thematic analysis yielded 128 items across 10 domains, 26 topics, and 92 issues. Experience of Care, notably user engagement and process costs, was most developed. Environmental Impact remained limited to carbon footprint and transparency.
 
 
 
 By highlighting key gaps, the review supports balanced, evidence-based DH decision-making and helps stakeholders prioritize innovations delivering technical, social and environmental value.
 
 
 
 This is the first systematic mapping of DH's social and environmental evaluation within the Sextuple Aim, resulting in a Holistic Impact Framework integrating underrepresented dimensions.

Title: Implementing Clinical Guidelines for the Treatment of Psychosis: The Frontline Leaders’ Point of View. A Qualitative Study
Snippet: Healthcare is commonly characterized as a Complex Adaptive System (CAS) recognized by a large set of interacting interdependent actors at the same or different organization levels or other organizations, which foster dynamic processes and complex working processes. 1,2 CAS evolves over time and in response to different stakeholders, system inputs and local contexts, highlighting an unpredictability when trying to implement new practices. 3 This constant evolution and instability may hinder standardization of working processes as intended by quality improvement and the translation of research findings into clinical practice. 4,5 On the other hand, the complexity and instability of the system can present opportunities for innovation and the implementation of new practices in healthcare. Therefore, we should embrace complexity, and engage and empower individuals and teams to constantly improve healthcare. 6 [9] Leadership in Complex Adaptive Systems Traditional leadership strategies, which include change management, are not well suited for CAS. 10,11 In a previous study exploring leadership strategies, we identified a broad range of leadership approaches that are currently used in implementation contexts, transcending traditional leadership strategies. 12 In light of CAS, leaders should embrace uncertainty, maintain a minimum of specifications, and adopt a constructive approach to variation. 13 Complexity Leadership Theory (CLT), which focuses on leaders promoting learning, creativity, and adaptively within the CAS organization, is highlighted by Uhl-Bien and Arena. 14,15 The CLT framework describes operational leadership as formal leadership for executing orders, entrepreneurial leadership as the source of new ideas, innovation, learning and growth for the organization and enabling leadership as promoting conditions that effectively support and sustain adaptive space. 14 Enabling leadership interacting with operational and entrepreneurial leadership approaches helps organizations to function as complex adaptive systems. 10,14

Title: Navigating complexity: a conceptual framework for simulation interventions
Snippet: Healthcare is inherently complex, characterized by interdependencies and unpredictable interactions [9][10][11]. Success depends on individual expertise and the system's ability to adapt to shifting constraints [12]. Complex Adaptive Systems theory has consistently provided insights into healthcare functioning beyond rigid structures. The theory views healthcare systems as networks of interacting agents whose behaviours are shaped by context and history [13,14]. Outcomes emerge through these interactions and cannot be fully understood by analyzing individual components in isolation. Rather than focusing on control, Complex Adaptive Systems theory emphasizes understanding and adaptation through continuous feedback and local decision-making [13,14]. Yet, many organizations still assume linear, reductionist approaches that prioritize predictable workflows over adaptability [15,16]. This misalignment hinders attempts to implement complexity-based strategies [17,18]. Healthcare involves multiple interacting elements, such as clinicians, patients, technology, and policies. These factors continuously shape system dynamics, influencing how teams respond to challenges, allocate resources, and maintain care quality [19][20][21]. 

Recognizing this need for adaptability, Resilient Healthcare builds on Complex Adaptive Systems principles, emphasizing flexibility over rigid error-reduction strategies to support quality and safety [1]. Resilient Healthcare acknowledges that variability in clinical work is inevitable, and that resilience stems from the ability to anticipate, respond to, and recover from disruptions [22]. Instead of treating variability as a risk, Resilient Healthcare highlights its role in maintaining safe and effective healthcare [22]. Understanding everyday work, including "workarounds, " guides improvement. As Nason notes, embracing complexity requires recognizing its characteristics and developing a mindset attuned to how complex systems behave [9]. Title: Strategic Pathways to Healthcare Excellence: A Review of Innovative Approaches for Improving Medical Services
Snippet: This review underscores that improving medical services is a complex but achievable goal when pursued through integrated, strategic pathways. Together, these elements create a synergistic ecosystem that fosters resilience, equity, and excellence in healthcare systems. 

Patient-centered and value-based care models ensure that services remain responsive to individual and community needs while aligning financial incentives with outcomes. Lean Six Sigma and workflow optimization strategies provide operational backbones for reducing waste and errors, thereby enhancing efficiency and safety. Meanwhile, digital health innovations such as telemedicine, electronic health records, and artificial intelligence expand access, support decision-making, and enable data-driven improvements. Yet, these tools must be deployed equitably to avoid exacerbating health disparities. 

Central to all improvement efforts is the healthcare workforce. Continuous education, leadership development, and interprofessional collaboration are critical for translating strategies into practice. Without an empowered and resilient workforce, even the most advanced technologies or policies will fail to achieve intended results. Additionally, effective governance and policy alignment are indispensable for scaling innovations, ensuring regulatory clarity, and embedding accountability mechanisms. 

The review also highlighted persistent barriers-financial constraints, organizational resistance, digital divides, and ethical complexities-that can hinder the adoption and sustainability of these strategies. Addressing such barriers requires not only institutional leadership but also national and international collaboration. Policymakers must provide resources and regulatory frameworks that promote innovation while safeguarding equity and ethics. 

Ultimately, the pursuit of healthcare excellence must be dynamic, adaptive, and patientfocused. As health systems confront emerging challenges-ranging from demographic shifts to technological disruptions-strategies must evolve accordingly. Future efforts should prioritize cross-sector collaboration, equity in access, and the integration of continuous learning mechanisms. 

By strategically aligning resources, processes, and policies, healthcare systems can move closer to achieving excellence in medical service delivery. Such a transformation not only improves quality and safety but also strengthens public trust and ensures that healthcare remains sustainable, resilient, and equitable for future generations.

Title: 'Complexity-compatible' policy for integrated care? Lessons from the implementation of Ontario's Health Links.
Snippet: Complex adaptive systems (CAS) theory views healthcare as numerous sub-systems characterized by diverse agents that interact, self-organize, and continuously adapt. We apply this complexity science perspective to examine the extent to which CAS theory is a useful lens for designing and implementing health policies. We present the case of Health Links, a "low rules" policy intervention in Ontario, Canada aimed at stimulating the development of voluntary networks of health and social organizations to improve care coordination for the most frequent users of the healthcare system. Our sample consisted of stakeholders from regional governance bodies and organizations partnering in Health Links. Qualitative interview data were coded using the key complexity concepts of sensemaking, self-organization, interconnections, coevolution, and emergence. We found that the complexity-compatible policy design successfully stimulated local dynamics of flexibility, experimentation, and learning and that important mediating factors include leadership, readiness, relationship-building, role clarity, communication, and resources. However, we saw tensions between preferences for flexibility and standardization. Desirable developments occurred only in some settings and failed to flow upward to higher levels, resulting in a piecemeal and patchy landscape. Attention needs to be paid not only to local dynamics and processes, but also to regional and provincial levels to ensure that learning flows to the top and informs decision-making. We conclude that implementation of complexity-compatible policies needs a balance between flexibility and consistency and the right leadership to coordinate the two. Complexity-compatible policy for integrated healthcare is more than simply 'letting a thousand flowers bloom'.

Snippet: Digital transformation in healthcare refers to the comprehensive process of integrating advanced digital technologies such as electronic health records (EHRs), telemedicine, data analytics, and remote monitoring into the organization's operations, workflows, and culture to enhance care delivery, operational efficiency, and patient outcomes (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022;Alanazi, 2022). Rather than merely digitizing existing practices, effective digital transformation implies rethinking how care is delivered, managed, and coordinated redefining roles, communication flows, decision-making pathways, and even organizational values (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022). The advent of technologies under the umbrella of Industry 4.0 The IoT, big data, cloud computing, and AI have accelerated this trend, rendering digital transformation a strategic necessity rather than optional innovation for modern healthcare institutions (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022;Alanazi, 2022). 

Despite its promise, digital transformation in healthcare is far from straightforward. Healthcare organizations operate in complex, high-stakes contexts where data security, patient safety, regulatory compliance, and ethical considerations are paramount. These contexts make implementation particularly challenging in technological readiness alone is insufficient (Kolukısa et al., 2020; Taher et al., 2025). In many settings, infrastructural constraints (e.g., limited internet connectivity or unstable power supply), insufficient IT resources, and lack of interoperability hinder consistent adoption of digital tools (Taher et al., 2025;Hameed & Hameed, 2023). In addition, human and organizational factors such as limited digital literacy, resistance to change, lack of training, and unclear governance structures often undermine efforts to integrate digital systems sustainably (Taher et al., 2025;Kaihlanen et al., 2025). Thus, digital transformation in healthcare must be approached not only as a technical upgrade but as a complex socio-organizational change process. 

In this light, leadership plays a central role in enabling and sustaining digital transformation in healthcare. Traditional leadership models may offer some value, but the digital context demands more: leaders need to combine vision, technical and digital competence, inclusive decision-making, and adaptability.

Title: Literature Review: Emerging Innovation Frontiers in Healthcare and Their Transformative Impact on Sustainability—Implications for Adoption Barriers and Leadership-Governance Dynamics

Introduction and Conceptual Framing
Healthcare systems worldwide are converging on an “innovation frontier” that spans digital technologies, artificial intelligence, value-based and population health models, integrated care platforms, and workforce and governance redesigns. Sustainability in this context is multidimensional: environmental (carbon, waste, energy), social (equity, patient experience, workforce well-being), and economic (cost efficiency, resilience). A mixed-method approach is needed because, while digitalization can deliver measurable gains in emissions, access, and cost, its system-wide sustainability depends on organizational readiness, governance quality, and adaptive decision-making that reconcile technical promise with human, workflow, and policy realities. <cite id="780532a3-0">Digitalization of care, including telemedicine and AI, can reduce sectoral environmental impacts yet introduces energy and e-waste burdens, demanding lifecycle-aware strategies aligned with planetary health goals</cite> <cite id="780532a3-3">Digital health impact assessments often emphasize experience and population health but underweight environmental and equity dimensions within value-based frameworks, signaling a need for holistic evaluation</cite>.

Emerging frontiers are coalescing around three pillars: (1) digitally enabled, data-driven care; (2) integrated and population-based delivery; and (3) adaptive governance and workforce models. <cite id="780532a3-0">Scoping across 58 studies shows telemedicine as the dominant digital vector for sustainability impacts, with most work quantifying transport emissions avoided and many reporting concurrent gains in patient experience, time efficiency, and cost</cite> <cite id="780532a3-3">A systematic mapping of digital health impact studies found that while experience of care and population health are frequently assessed, environmental and equity outcomes remain marginal, reinforcing the need to balance technical and social aims</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-3">A Holistic Impact Framework integrating underrepresented social and environmental dimensions complements the Triple Aim and provides a planning scaffold for mixed-method evaluations</cite>.

Digital Technologies and Sustainable Healthcare: Environmental, Social, and Economic Effects
Environmental effects
Digitalization can cut greenhouse gas emissions by displacing travel and consolidating care. <cite id="780532a3-0">Across 58 studies, 91% focused on telemedicine; 97% quantified transport-related emissions reductions, with total avoided emissions estimated at approximately 830 million kg CO2</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-0">However, only 12% evaluated full life cycle impacts, underscoring the risk that energy-intensive infrastructure and device manufacturing erode environmental benefits</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-1">Digital tools may reduce some environmental footprints but can also increase energy use through rebound effects and by expanding digital infrastructures; adoption without behavioral or systemic change can leave environmental outcomes unchanged</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-2">Health systems’ dual roles as climate responders and drivers mandate aligning digitalization with environmental goals and policy to avoid contradictions between growth and sustainability</cite>.

Social effects
Digital care often improves patient-centered experience and care coordination. <cite id="780532a3-0">A majority of studies emphasized higher satisfaction, time efficiency, and convenience, alongside reduced burden for caregivers</cite>. <cite id="780532a3-3">Digital health assessments increasingly capture experience-of-care and population health while offering tools to embed equity into design, yet environmental and transparency dimensions remain limited</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Organizational readiness and change management mediate whether digital tools translate into daily practice; leadership that shapes culture and involvement reduces resistance among older, less engaged staff and improves sustained use</cite>.

<cite id="320e7d7f-0">Even with leadership commitment, digital tools can feel burdensome when excluded from design or perceived as useless; generational and role-fit mismatches reduce engagement and sustain low utilization</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-0">Older staff frequently perceive EHRs as irrelevant to their roles, signaling gaps in user involvement and change management that impede behavioral adoption despite technological availability</cite>. <cite id="320e7d7f-4">Across settings, interoperability deficits, limited digital literacy, resistance to change, and unclear governance structures undermine consistent, safe integration of digital systems</cite>.

Leadership Mindsets, Governance Styles, and Adaptive Decision-Making as Catalysts or Bottlenecks

Implications for Mixed-Methods Research and Practice

Governance diagnostics and adaptive evaluation
<cite id="451d5c01-4">Complexity-compatible governance should monitor both local learning dynamics and vertical translation of lessons; balancing flexibility and consistency under capable leadership prevents patchy diffusion and blocked scaling</cite>. <cite id="451d5c01-1">Adopting resilient-healthcare principles—continuous feedback loops, local decision-making, and workarounds-as-data—supports adaptive evaluation that distinguishes true system change from superficial workflow digitization</cite>.

Proposed Contributions of the Mixed-Methods Study

Conclusions and Research Agenda
Digital technologies are reshaping healthcare’s environmental, social, and economic footprints, but their sustainability is contingent on governance that integrates lifecycle impacts, equity, and adaptive capacity. <cite id="780532a3-0">Telemedicine can avoid hundreds of thousands of metric tons of CO2 while improving experience and costs, yet benefits depend on lifecycle analyses and governance that constrains rebound and infrastructure lock-in</cite> <cite id="780532a3-1">Digitalization may also increase energy and resource use if adoption is not matched by systemic and behavioral change</cite>. Title: Aligning With the Goals of the Planetary Health Concept Regarding Ecological Sustainability and Digital Health: Scoping Review
Snippet: Background Climate change, driven by greenhouse gas emissions, threatens human health and biodiversity. While the digitalization of health care, including telemedicine and artificial intelligence, offers sustainability benefits, it also raises concerns about energy use and electronic waste. Balancing these factors is key to a sustainable health care future. Objective The objective of this review was to examine the extent to which digitalization in the health care sector influences environmental sustainability. Specifically, it aimed to assess how digitalization can contribute to reducing the health care sector’s impact on global climate change. From these findings, conclusions were drawn regarding the extent to which digitalization aligns with the objectives of the Planetary Health movement and how these 2 movements may mutually reinforce each other. Methods A scoping review guided by the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines using databases such as PubMed and Scopus was conducted, and 58 quantitative studies from 2009 to 2024 were analyzed for environmental, social, and economic outcomes aligned with Planetary Health goals. Results This review analyzed 58 studies on the environmental impact of digitalization in health care primarily focusing on telemedicine, which was examined in 91% (53/58) of the studies. Most studies (56/58, 97%) quantified transport-related emissions avoided through digitalization, with some also assessing emissions from health care facilities, medical equipment, and energy consumption. Findings indicated that telemedicine significantly reduces carbon dioxide emissions, with total avoided emissions amounting to approximately 830 million kg. A substantial proportion of the studies (36/58, 62%) focused on social aspects, highlighting factors such as patient satisfaction, time efficiency, and overall convenience. In addition, economic considerations were analyzed in 48% (28/58) of the studies, emphasizing cost reductions and resource optimization. However, only 12% (7/58) of the studies evaluated the full life cycle impact of digital technologies, highlighting the need for further research on their long-term environmental sustainability. Conclusions This review calls for further research beyond telemedicine, advocating for life cycle analyses and actionable strategies for a sustainable digitalization in health care systems. The Planetary Health framework is highlighted as a guide for ensuring sustainable digital transformation in health care.

Title: Why digital innovation may not alleviate healthcare’s environmental impacts
Snippet: Healthcare is becoming increasingly digitalised through innovations in information and communication technologies, including monitoring devices, streaming, data storage, and increasingly through advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) (1). Advocates enthuse that this digitalisation will improve key aspects of healthcare delivery, including enhanced safety, accessibility, quality of care, effectiveness, and efficiency (2). Others debate whether these promises can be met because of complex social, cultural, economic, and political implementation challenges (3). snippet.text: Background Climate change, driven by greenhouse gas emissions, threatens human health and biodiversity. While the digitalization of health care, including telemedicine and artificial intelligence, offers sustainability benefits, it also raises concerns about energy use and electronic waste. Balancing these factors is key to a sustainable health care future. Objective The objective of this review was to examine the extent to which digitalization in the health care sector influences environmental sustainability. Specifically, it aimed to assess how digitalization can contribute to reducing the health care sector’s impact on global climate change. From these findings, conclusions were drawn regarding the extent to which digitalization aligns with the objectives of the Planetary Health movement and how these 2 movements may mutually reinforce each other. Methods A scoping review guided by the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines using databases such as PubMed and Scopus was conducted, and 58 quantitative studies from 2009 to 2024 were analyzed for environmental, social, and economic outcomes aligned with Planetary Health goals. Results This review analyzed 58 studies on the environmental impact of digitalization in health care primarily focusing on telemedicine, which was examined in 91% (53/58) of the studies. Most studies (56/58, 97%) quantified transport-related emissions avoided through digitalization, with some also assessing emissions from health care facilities, medical equipment, and energy consumption. Findings indicated that telemedicine significantly reduces carbon dioxide emissions, with total avoided emissions amounting to approximately 830 million kg. A substantial proportion of the studies (36/58, 62%) focused on social aspects, highlighting factors such as patient satisfaction, time efficiency, and overall convenience. In addition, economic considerations were analyzed in 48% (28/58) of the studies, emphasizing cost reductions and resource optimization. However, only 12% (7/58) of the studies evaluated the full life cycle impact of digital technologies, highlighting the need for further research on their long-term environmental sustainability. Conclusions This review calls for further research beyond telemedicine, advocating for life cycle analyses and actionable strategies for a sustainable digitalization in health care systems. The Planetary Health framework is highlighted as a guide for ensuring sustainable digital transformation in health care.

Title: Implementing Clinical Guidelines for the Treatment of Psychosis: The Frontline Leaders’ Point of View. A Qualitative Study
Snippet: Healthcare is commonly characterized as a Complex Adaptive System (CAS) recognized by a large set of interacting interdependent actors at the same or different organization levels or other organizations, which foster dynamic processes and complex working processes. 1,2 CAS evolves over time and in response to different stakeholders, system inputs and local contexts, highlighting an unpredictability when trying to implement new practices. 3 This constant evolution and instability may hinder standardization of working processes as intended by quality improvement and the translation of research findings into clinical practice. 4,5 On the other hand, the complexity and instability of the system can present opportunities for innovation and the implementation of new practices in healthcare. Therefore, we should embrace complexity, and engage and empower individuals and teams to constantly improve healthcare. 6 [9] Leadership in Complex Adaptive Systems Traditional leadership strategies, which include change management, are not well suited for CAS. 10,11 In a previous study exploring leadership strategies, we identified a broad range of leadership approaches that are currently used in implementation contexts, transcending traditional leadership strategies. 12 In light of CAS, leaders should embrace uncertainty, maintain a minimum of specifications, and adopt a constructive approach to variation. 13 Complexity Leadership Theory (CLT), which focuses on leaders promoting learning, creativity, and adaptively within the CAS organization, is highlighted by Uhl-Bien and Arena. 14,15 The CLT framework describes operational leadership as formal leadership for executing orders, entrepreneurial leadership as the source of new ideas, innovation, learning and growth for the organization and enabling leadership as promoting conditions that effectively support and sustain adaptive space. 14 Enabling leadership interacting with operational and entrepreneurial leadership approaches helps organizations to function as complex adaptive systems. 10,14

Title: Navigating complexity: a conceptual framework for simulation interventions
Snippet: Healthcare is inherently complex, characterized by interdependencies and unpredictable interactions [9][10][11]. Success depends on individual expertise and the system's ability to adapt to shifting constraints [12]. Complex Adaptive Systems theory has consistently provided insights into healthcare functioning beyond rigid structures. The theory views healthcare systems as networks of interacting agents whose behaviours are shaped by context and history [13,14]. Outcomes emerge through these interactions and cannot be fully understood by analyzing individual components in isolation. Rather than focusing on control, Complex Adaptive Systems theory emphasizes understanding and adaptation through continuous feedback and local decision-making [13,14]. Yet, many organizations still assume linear, reductionist approaches that prioritize predictable workflows over adaptability [15,16]. This misalignment hinders attempts to implement complexity-based strategies [17,18]. Healthcare involves multiple interacting elements, such as clinicians, patients, technology, and policies. These factors continuously shape system dynamics, influencing how teams respond to challenges, allocate resources, and maintain care quality [19][20][21]. 

Recognizing this need for adaptability, Resilient Healthcare builds on Complex Adaptive Systems principles, emphasizing flexibility over rigid error-reduction strategies to support quality and safety [1]. Resilient Healthcare acknowledges that variability in clinical work is inevitable, and that resilience stems from the ability to anticipate, respond to, and recover from disruptions [22]. Instead of treating variability as a risk, Resilient Healthcare highlights its role in maintaining safe and effective healthcare [22]. Understanding everyday work, including "workarounds, " guides improvement. As Nason notes, embracing complexity requires recognizing its characteristics and developing a mindset attuned to how complex systems behave [9]. In healthcare leadership, this mindset rarely arises from awareness alone. It tends to evolve through sustained engagement with system-level challenges and practical experience with clinical work's unpredictable and adaptive nature [9]. Table 1 presents selected examples of influential resources on Complex Adaptive Systems and Resilient Healthcare, each with a brief description.

Title: Strategic Pathways to Healthcare Excellence: A Review of Innovative Approaches for Improving Medical Services
Snippet: This review underscores that improving medical services is a complex but achievable goal when pursued through integrated, strategic pathways. The evidence demonstrates that no single intervention is sufficient to transform healthcare delivery; instead, sustainable improvement requires a holistic approach combining patient-centered models, operational efficiency, digital health innovations, workforce development, and supportive policy frameworks. Together, these elements create a synergistic ecosystem that fosters resilience, equity, and excellence in healthcare systems. 

Patient-centered and value-based care models ensure that services remain responsive to individual and community needs while aligning financial incentives with outcomes. Lean Six Sigma and workflow optimization strategies provide operational backbones for reducing waste and errors, thereby enhancing efficiency and safety. Meanwhile, digital health innovations such as telemedicine, electronic health records, and artificial intelligence expand access, support decision-making, and enable data-driven improvements. Yet, these tools must be deployed equitably to avoid exacerbating health disparities. 

Central to all improvement efforts is the healthcare workforce. Continuous education, leadership development, and interprofessional collaboration are critical for translating strategies into practice. Without an empowered and resilient workforce, even the most advanced technologies or policies will fail to achieve intended results. Additionally, effective governance and policy alignment are indispensable for scaling innovations, ensuring regulatory clarity, and embedding accountability mechanisms. 

The review also highlighted persistent barriers-financial constraints, organizational resistance, digital divides, and ethical complexities-that can hinder the adoption and sustainability of these strategies. Addressing such barriers requires not only institutional leadership but also national and international collaboration. Policymakers must provide resources and regulatory frameworks that promote innovation while safeguarding equity and ethics. 

Ultimately, the pursuit of healthcare excellence must be dynamic, adaptive, and patientfocused. As health systems confront emerging challenges-ranging from demographic shifts to technological disruptions-strategies must evolve accordingly. Future efforts should prioritize cross-sector collaboration, equity in access, and the integration of continuous learning mechanisms. 

By strategically aligning resources, processes, and policies, healthcare systems can move closer to achieving excellence in medical service delivery. Such a transformation not only improves quality and safety but also strengthens public trust and ensures that healthcare remains sustainable, resilient, and equitable for future generations.

Title: Pillars of Organizational Transformation and Sustainability: Leadership, Learning, Culture, and Knowledge Management as Key Success Factors in Environmental Public Health
Snippet: Adaptive leadership provides the tools needed to navigate the uncertain and complex landscapes that define sustainability challenges. Heifetz et al. (2009) emphasize the role of leaders in mobilizing people to confront challenges, experiment with solutions, and thrive amid change. Adaptive leadership is particularly relevant in environmental public health, where the dynamic nature of climate change, emerging diseases, and resource constraints necessitates innovative and flexible approaches. This model encourages public health leaders to experiment with new strategies, collaborate across disciplines, and build resilience to address evolving environmental risks (Dugan, 2017). For example, adaptive leadership underpins efforts to develop climate-resilient healthcare infrastructure and to design public health interventions that can respond to shifting environmental threats. 

Integrating these leadership models into both organizational transformation and environmental public health systems highlights their shared need for innovation, inclusivity, and resilience. Transformational, servant, and adaptive leaderships provide complementary frameworks that empower leaders to address the interconnected challenges of sustainability while fostering long-term success in an evolving global context.

Title: 'Complexity-compatible' policy for integrated care? Lessons from the implementation of Ontario's Health Links.
Snippet: Complex adaptive systems (CAS) theory views healthcare as numerous sub-systems characterized by diverse agents that interact, self-organize, and continuously adapt. We apply this complexity science perspective to examine the extent to which CAS theory is a useful lens for designing and implementing health policies. We present the case of Health Links, a "low rules" policy intervention in Ontario, Canada aimed at stimulating the development of voluntary networks of health and social organizations to improve care coordination for the most frequent users of the healthcare system. Our sample consisted of stakeholders from regional governance bodies and organizations partnering in Health Links. Qualitative interview data were coded using the key complexity concepts of sensemaking, self-organization, interconnections, coevolution, and emergence. We found that the complexity-compatible policy design successfully stimulated local dynamics of flexibility, experimentation, and learning and that important mediating factors include leadership, readiness, relationship-building, role clarity, communication, and resources. However, we saw tensions between preferences for flexibility and standardization. Desirable developments occurred only in some settings and failed to flow upward to higher levels, resulting in a piecemeal and patchy landscape. snippet.text:
Healthcare is inherently complex, characterized by interdependencies and unpredictable interactions [9][10][11]. Success depends on individual expertise and the system's ability to adapt to shifting constraints [12]. Complex Adaptive Systems theory has consistently provided insights into healthcare functioning beyond rigid structures. The theory views healthcare systems as networks of interacting agents whose behaviours are shaped by context and history [13,14]. Outcomes emerge through these interactions and cannot be fully understood by analyzing individual components in isolation. Rather than focusing on control, Complex Adaptive Systems theory emphasizes understanding and adaptation through continuous feedback and local decision-making [13,14]. Yet, many organizations still assume linear, reductionist approaches that prioritize predictable workflows over adaptability [15,16]. This misalignment hinders attempts to implement complexity-based strategies [17,18]. Healthcare involves multiple interacting elements, such as clinicians, patients, technology, and policies. These factors continuously shape system dynamics, influencing how teams respond to challenges, allocate resources, and maintain care quality [19][20][21]. 

Recognizing this need for adaptability, Resilient Healthcare builds on Complex Adaptive Systems principles, emphasizing flexibility over rigid error-reduction strategies to support quality and safety [1]. Resilient Healthcare acknowledges that variability in clinical work is inevitable, and that resilience stems from the ability to anticipate, respond to, and recover from disruptions [22]. Instead of treating variability as a risk, Resilient Healthcare highlights its role in maintaining safe and effective healthcare [22]. Understanding everyday work, including "workarounds, " guides improvement. As Nason notes, embracing complexity requires recognizing its characteristics and developing a mindset attuned to how complex systems behave [9]. In healthcare leadership, this mindset rarely arises from awareness alone. It tends to evolve through sustained engagement with system-level challenges and practical experience with clinical work's unpredictable and adaptive nature [9]. snippet.text:
This review underscores that improving medical services is a complex but achievable goal when pursued through integrated, strategic pathways. The evidence demonstrates that no single intervention is sufficient to transform healthcare delivery; instead, sustainable improvement requires a holistic approach combining patient-centered models, operational efficiency, digital health innovations, workforce development, and supportive policy frameworks. Together, these elements create a synergistic ecosystem that fosters resilience, equity, and excellence in healthcare systems. 

Patient-centered and value-based care models ensure that services remain responsive to individual and community needs while aligning financial incentives with outcomes. Lean Six Sigma and workflow optimization strategies provide operational backbones for reducing waste and errors, thereby enhancing efficiency and safety. Meanwhile, digital health innovations such as telemedicine, electronic health records, and artificial intelligence expand access, support decision-making, and enable data-driven improvements. Yet, these tools must be deployed equitably to avoid exacerbating health disparities. 

Central to all improvement efforts is the healthcare workforce. Continuous education, leadership development, and interprofessional collaboration are critical for translating strategies into practice. Without an empowered and resilient workforce, even the most advanced technologies or policies will fail to achieve intended results. Additionally, effective governance and policy alignment are indispensable for scaling innovations, ensuring regulatory clarity, and embedding accountability mechanisms. 

The review also highlighted persistent barriers-financial constraints, organizational resistance, digital divides, and ethical complexities-that can hinder the adoption and sustainability of these strategies. Addressing such barriers requires not only institutional leadership but also national and international collaboration. Policymakers must provide resources and regulatory frameworks that promote innovation while safeguarding equity and ethics. 

Ultimately, the pursuit of healthcare excellence must be dynamic, adaptive, and patientfocused. As health systems confront emerging challenges-ranging from demographic shifts to technological disruptions-strategies must evolve accordingly. Future efforts should prioritize cross-sector collaboration, equity in access, and the integration of continuous learning mechanisms. 

By strategically aligning resources, processes, and policies, healthcare systems can move closer to achieving excellence in medical service delivery. Such a transformation not only improves quality and safety but also strengthens public trust and ensures that healthcare remains sustainable, resilient, and equitable for future generations.

snippet.text:
Adaptive leadership provides the tools needed to navigate the uncertain and complex landscapes that define sustainability challenges. Heifetz et al. (2009) emphasize the role of leaders in mobilizing people to confront challenges, experiment with solutions, and thrive amid change. Adaptive leadership is particularly relevant in environmental public health, where the dynamic nature of climate change, emerging diseases, and resource constraints necessitates innovative and flexible approaches. This model encourages public health leaders to experiment with new strategies, collaborate across disciplines, and build resilience to address evolving environmental risks (Dugan, 2017). For example, adaptive leadership underpins efforts to develop climate-resilient healthcare infrastructure and to design public health interventions that can respond to shifting environmental threats. 

Integrating these leadership models into both organizational transformation and environmental public health systems highlights their shared need for innovation, inclusivity, and resilience. Transformational, servant, and adaptive leaderships provide complementary frameworks that empower leaders to address the interconnected challenges of sustainability while fostering long-term success in an evolving global context.

snippet.text: Complex adaptive systems (CAS) theory views healthcare as numerous sub-systems characterized by diverse agents that interact, self-organize, and continuously adapt. We apply this complexity science perspective to examine the extent to which CAS theory is a useful lens for designing and implementing health policies. We present the case of Health Links, a "low rules" policy intervention in Ontario, Canada aimed at stimulating the development of voluntary networks of health and social organizations to improve care coordination for the most frequent users of the healthcare system. Our sample consisted of stakeholders from regional governance bodies and organizations partnering in Health Links. Qualitative interview data were coded using the key complexity concepts of sensemaking, self-organization, interconnections, coevolution, and emergence. We found that the complexity-compatible policy design successfully stimulated local dynamics of flexibility, experimentation, and learning and that important mediating factors include leadership, readiness, relationship-building, role clarity, communication, and resources. However, we saw tensions between preferences for flexibility and standardization. Desirable developments occurred only in some settings and failed to flow upward to higher levels, resulting in a piecemeal and patchy landscape. Attention needs to be paid not only to local dynamics and processes, but also to regional and provincial levels to ensure that learning flows to the top and informs decision-making. We conclude that implementation of complexity-compatible policies needs a balance between flexibility and consistency and the right leadership to coordinate the two. Complexity-compatible policy for integrated healthcare is more than simply 'letting a thousand flowers bloom'.

Title: Factors influencing electronic health record system use in public health facilities in Tanzania
Snippet: Similar patterns have been reported in empirical studies by Helminski et al. [53] and Melnick et al. [51], which found that leadership influences system acceptance indirectly by shaping institutional culture and performance expectations. Thus, even when leadership does not emerge as a quantitative predictor, its qualitative influence remains fundamental to sustaining EHR use. 

The analysis also revealed motivational and generational differences among staff. Older employees, in particular, perceived the EHR system as burdensome or irrelevant to their professional roles. This mirrors findings by Provenzano et al. [46], who noted that exclusion from system design and low perceived usefulness can foster disengagement. From a TOE perspective, this represents a weakness in the organizational dimension, specifically, limited user involvement and change-management planning, that impedes the translation of technological potential into behavioral adoption. 

These findings confirm that organizational readiness is the cornerstone of EHR implementation success. Facilities that cultivate strong leadership, embed digital workflows, and invest in sustained capacity-building are better positioned to overcome technological or environmental constraints. Strengthening these elements enhances not only EHR utilization but also the organization's ability to innovate and adapt to evolving digital health reforms.

Title: Policy Innovations and Organisational Change in Health Informatics: A Qualitative Review of Strategies for Effective System Enhancement
Snippet: Health informatics systems are rapidly evolving, driven by emerging technologies and shifting policy landscapes. Despite substantial advancements, challenges in effective system implementation persist, particularly in policy innovation and organizational change. This study aims to qualitatively review strategies that enhance health informatics systems through policy and organizational interventions. A qualitative literature review method was employed, systematically analyzing 80 relevant peer-reviewed articles, policy reports, and institutional documents published between 2015 and 2025. Data were collected through purposive searches in major academic databases, including Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect. The inclusion criteria focused on studies addressing policy innovation, organizational change, interoperability, workforce capacity, and stakeholder engagement in health informatics. Thematic analysis was conducted to identify key patterns and relationships across the selected literature. Results indicate that integrated policy frameworks combined with proactive organizational readiness significantly improve digital health adoption, interoperability, and data governance. Leadership commitment, workforce capacity building, and multi-sector stakeholder engagement emerged as critical enablers. The review also highlights the importance of adaptive strategies tailored to diverse resource settings for sustainable system enhancement. In conclusion, effective health informatics system enhancement requires holistic approaches that align policy innovation with organizational transformation and stakeholder collaboration

Title: INTEGRATING TRANSFORMATIONAL, PARTICIPATIVE, AND DIGITAL LEADERSHIP FOR EFFECTIVE HEALTHCARE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
Snippet: Digital transformation in healthcare encompasses the integration of digital technologies such as electronic health records (EHRs), telehealth platforms, mobile health applications, and data analytics into clinical and administrative workflows to improve quality, efficiency, and patientcentered outcomes ( Leadership plays a pivotal role in overcoming these challenges and enabling successful digital transformation. Leaders who combine strategic vision, digital literacy, and the ability to inspire and engage staff can foster an organizational climate conducive to innovation and change (Alanazi, 2022;Keesara et al., 2020). Transformational leadership can motivate employees to embrace new technologies, participative leadership ensures inclusion and shared ownership of change processes, and digital leadership provides the necessary expertise to guide technology adoption effectively (Alanazi, 2022). By aligning technological, cultural, and human factors, capable leadership serves as the critical enabler for adoption, innovation, and sustainable improvement in healthcare delivery.

Title: Nursing Leadership for Digital NICU Transformation: A Systematic Review of Strategies, Digital Health Integration, and Outcomes in High-Risk Neonates
Snippet: This gap is consequential because poorly governed digital change can amplify workload, alert fatigue, and safety risks, while widening inequities in access and family engagement. Broader literature from other high-stakes healthcare contexts similarly highlights the importance of leadership competencies and ethical governance for complex system change (Alruwaili et al., 2025a;Fischer et al., 2024;Grimell & Nilsson, 2020;Malterud et al., 2016;Ramadan, Aldousari, et al., 2025;Ramadan, Alshammari, et al., 2025). 

This review addressed that gap by: (1) identifying nursing leadership models, strategies, and actions used to integrate digital health in NICUs; (2) cataloging implemented technologies and workflow integration approaches; (3) mapping implementation frameworks and evidence-based strategies; (4) examining associations between leadership approaches and implementation, clinical, and family/workforce outcomes; and (5) distilling facilitators, barriers, and best practices for nursing-led digital transformation in neonatal intensive care. Practically, the review was intended to provide nurse leaders, NICU managers, educators, and policymakers with actionable levers for planning, staffing, training, and evaluating digital NICU transformation.

Title: INTEGRATING TRANSFORMATIONAL, PARTICIPATIVE, AND DIGITAL LEADERSHIP FOR EFFECTIVE HEALTHCARE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
Snippet: Digital transformation in healthcare refers to the comprehensive process of integrating advanced digital technologies such as electronic health records (EHRs), telemedicine, data analytics, and remote monitoring into the organization's operations, workflows, and culture to enhance care delivery, operational efficiency, and patient outcomes (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022;Alanazi, 2022). Rather than merely digitizing existing practices, effective digital transformation implies rethinking how care is delivered, managed, and coordinated redefining roles, communication flows, decision-making pathways, and even organizational values (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022). The advent of technologies under the umbrella of Industry 4.0 The IoT, big data, cloud computing, and AI have accelerated this trend, rendering digital transformation a strategic necessity rather than optional innovation for modern healthcare institutions (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022;Alanazi, 2022). 

Despite its promise, digital transformation in healthcare is far from straightforward. Healthcare organizations operate in complex, high-stakes contexts where data security, patient safety, regulatory compliance, and ethical considerations are paramount. These contexts make implementation particularly challenging in technological readiness alone is insufficient (Kolukısa et al., 2020; Taher et al., 2025). In many settings, infrastructural constraints (e.g., limited internet connectivity or unstable power supply), insufficient IT resources, and lack of interoperability hinder consistent adoption of digital tools (Taher et al., 2025;Hameed & Hameed, 2023). In addition, human and organizational factors such as limited digital literacy, resistance to change, lack of training, and unclear governance structures often undermine efforts to integrate digital systems sustainably (Taher et al., 2025;Kaihlanen et al., 2025). Thus, digital transformation in healthcare must be approached not only as a technical upgrade but as a complex socio-organizational change process. 

In this light, leadership plays a central role in enabling and sustaining digital transformation in healthcare. Traditional leadership models may offer some value, but the digital context demands more: leaders need to combine vision, technical and digital competence, inclusive decision-making, and adaptability.

The advent of technologies under the umbrella of Industry 4.0 The IoT, big data, cloud computing, and AI have accelerated this trend, rendering digital transformation a strategic necessity rather than optional innovation for modern healthcare institutions (Ahsan & Siddique, 2022;Alanazi, 2022). 

Despite its promise, digital transformation in healthcare is far from straightforward. Healthcare organizations operate in complex, high-stakes contexts where data security, patient safety, regulatory compliance, and ethical considerations are paramount. These contexts make implementation particularly challenging in technological readiness alone is insufficient (Kolukısa et al., 2020; Taher et al., 2025). In many settings, infrastructural constraints (e.g., limited internet connectivity or unstable power supply), insufficient IT resources, and lack of interoperability hinder consistent adoption of digital tools (Taher et al., 2025;Hameed & Hameed, 2023). In addition, human and organizational factors such as limited digital literacy, resistance to change, lack of training, and unclear governance structures often undermine efforts to integrate digital systems sustainably (Taher et al., 2025;Kaihlanen et al., 2025). Thus, digital transformation in healthcare must be approached not only as a technical upgrade but as a complex socio-organizational change process. 

In this light, leadership plays a central role in enabling and sustaining digital transformation in healthcare. Traditional leadership models may offer some value, but the digital context demands more: leaders need to combine vision, technical and digital competence, inclusive decision-making, and adaptability.

Thus, even when leadership does not emerge as a quantitative predictor, its qualitative influence remains fundamental to sustaining EHR use.

This mirrors findings by Provenzano et al. [46], who noted that exclusion from system design and low perceived usefulness can foster disengagement. Strengthening these elements enhances not only EHR utilization but also the organization's ability to innovate and adapt to evolving digital health reforms.

documents.title: Policy Innovations and Organisational Change in Health Informatics: A Qualitative Review of Strategies for Effective System Enhancement
documents.snippet: Health informatics systems are rapidly evolving, driven by emerging technologies and shifting policy landscapes. Despite substantial advancements, challenges in effective system implementation persist, particularly in policy innovation and organizational change. This study aims to qualitatively review strategies that enhance health informatics systems through policy and organizational interventions. A qualitative literature review method was employed, systematically analyzing 80 relevant peer-reviewed articles, policy reports, and institutional documents published between 2015 and 2025. Data were collected through purposive searches in major academic databases, including Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect. The inclusion criteria focused on studies addressing policy innovation, organizational change, interoperability, workforce capacity, and stakeholder engagement in health informatics. Thematic analysis was conducted to identify key patterns and relationships across the selected literature. Results indicate that integrated policy frameworks combined with proactive organizational readiness significantly improve digital health adoption, interoperability, and data governance. Leadership commitment, workforce capacity building, and multi-sector stakeholder engagement emerged as critical enablers. The review also highlights the importance of adaptive strategies tailored to diverse resource settings for sustainable system enhancement. In conclusion, effective health informatics system enhancement requires holistic approaches that align policy innovation with organizational transformation and stakeholder collaboration
