Title: A roadmap for developing a program to self-manage post-traumatic knee osteoarthritis risk
Snippet: CFIR is a widely used implementation science framework [27,33] for identifying, organizing, and assessing contextual factors that work for and against implementation of an innovation (e.g., new clinical program) across contexts [33]. We chose CFIR as an organizing framework to describe SOAR program development given that research focused solely on assessing the effectiveness of complex interventions [25,34] (multiple interacting components targeting a range of behaviours, outcomes, target groups, or implementation settings) often fails to deliver acceptable, feasible and scalable solutions [35][36][37], contributing to the underuse of effective health care solutions [38]. 

CFIR consists of 5 domains: Innovation, Inner setting, Outer setting, Individuals, and Implementation Process (Supplemental File 1) [33]. Briefly, the Innovation domain refers to the new program that continues after implementation (e.g., SOAR program) including its source, evidence-base, design, adaptability (ability to modify or tailor to fit local contexts), trialability (ability to test or pilot on a small scale), and cost. Inner Setting refers to the setting where the innovation is implemented (e. g., fee for service physiotherapy clinic), while the Outer Setting refers to the setting the inner setting exists within (e.g., provincial health system). The Individuals domain describes the roles and characteristics of individuals linked to the innovation (e.g., patients and physiotherapists), while the Implementation Process domain refers to the process framework [39] and/or activities and strategies [40] used to implement an innovation. 

CFIR is a pragmatic framework that allows researchers to select the most relevant domain(s) to describe or evaluate an innovation, implementation context, implementation process, or research findings. Because it is an overarching framework, CFIR can act as a scaffold for other implementation and behavioural science theories and models (e. g., COM-B [41]), reporting guidelines (e.g., Template for Intervention Description and Replication; TiDier [42,43]), or frameworks (e.g., Knowledge-to-Action Cycle [44], RE-AIM [45]).

Title: The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) User Guide: a five-step guide for conducting implementation research using the framework
Snippet: The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) is a determinant framework that includes constructs from many implementation theories, models, and frameworks [1][2][3]. The overarching aim of CFIR is to predict or explain barriers and facilitators (i.e., the determinants or independent variables) to implementation success (i.e., the outcome or dependent variable). CFIR includes 48 constructs and 19 subconstructs (i.e., determinants) across 5 broad domains: 1) Innovation; 2) Outer Setting; 3) Inner Setting; 4) Individuals: Roles & Characteristics; and 5) Implementation Process [2]. It has been cited over 10,000 times and is among the most widely applied implementation science frameworks [4]. Advances in research rely on users critically reflecting on and refining theories, models, and frameworks [5], and after 15 years of use in the field, CFIR was revised based on user feedback obtained via literature review and survey. The updated CFIR and accompanying CFIR outcomes addendum (Fig. 1) were published in 2022 [2,6]; updates are described in the Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) (see FAQ 1: How did CFIR change in the 2022 update?). In addition to changes to the framework, the original CFIR development team expanded into a larger CFIR Leadership Team (CLT), consisting of implementation scientists with a wealth of experience applying CFIR in their own projects as well as training others to use CFIR. CLT members come from a variety of disciplines, including public health, health promotion, evidence-based healthcare, psychology, social work, medicine, and anthropology. The CLT meets twice a month with the goal advancing CFIR scholarship and recently secured a 3-year grant from the Veterans Affairs (VA) Quality Enhancement Research Initiative (QUERI) Fig. 1 The CFIR Outcomes Addendum*.*This figure has been adapted from the original publication to highlight where Innovation Recipient Reach occurs within the CFIR Outcomes Addendum conceptualization of outcomes to create a CFIR "learning hub, " which will provide trainings, consultations, and mentoring for VA researchers and practitioners.

Title: Evaluating CFIR 2.0 in identifying digital twin implementation challenges in healthcare: bridging the dichotomy between engineering and healthcare communities
Snippet: The Implementation Science (IS) community offers numerous frameworks to guide researchers and practitioners in the adoption, integration, and evaluation of evidence-based interventions in healthcare settings (69). Frameworks like the CFIR (28), the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) (70), the Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services (PARiHS) (71), the Ecological framework, and the Non-Adoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread, and Sustainability (NASSS) framework (72) offer comprehensive lenses to analyze the intertwined factors in uencing intervention success (69). These frameworks emphasize the dynamic interplay between the organizational context, external environment, and individual stakeholder attributes, and the interaction of these with intervention characteristics. For example, the CFIR organizes these factors into five domains, offering a structured approach to identifying barriers and facilitators. Similarly, RE-AIM focuses on evaluating the public health impact of interventions by assessing reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation fidelity, and longterm maintenance, making it particularly useful for balancing internal and external validity. 

Here, it is useful to emphasize that these frameworks are not mutually exclusive but rather complementary in terms of addressing different implementation challenges. For instance, the PARiHS highlights the role of evidence, context, and facilitation in driving successful implementation, making it particularly useful in healthcare settings where stakeholder engagement and organizational readiness are critical (73). On the other hand, the NASSS addresses the complexity of scaling health technologies by examining domains such as the condition being treated, the technology itself, and the wider socio-political context, providing insights into why interventions may fail or succeed in real-world scenarios (74). Synergistic use of these frameworks could lead to a more holistic understanding of the factors in uencing implementation, enabling to design of implementation strategies that are effective, adaptable, and sustainable in diverse settings (75). 

CFIR is a framework designed to identify key factors in uencing the implementation of healthcare interventions. It is structured around five domains: intervention characteristics, outer setting, inner setting, characteristics of individuals, and the implementation process. Each of these domains encompasses a wide range of constructs that shape how interventions are adopted, implemented, and sustained within HSs.

Title: Exploring health equity integration among health service and delivery systems in Nova Scotia: perspectives of health system partners
Snippet: The ways that health equity is integrated into the different components of the health service and delivery system can be better understood through the lens of Implementation Science (IS). IS has been defined as the study of methods to promote the adoption and integration of evidence-based health interventions (e.g., tools, programs, and policies) into practice [12]. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) is a commonly used IS framework that can guide the systematic assessment of multi-level implementation contexts to identify or explain barriers and facilitators that might influence intervention implementation and effectiveness [13]. The CFIR is comprised of 39 constructs that operate across five domains (Innovation, Outer Setting, Inner Setting, Individuals, and Process) [13]. The CFIR has been applied to a range of contexts within health systems, ranging from individual programs to improve service delivery, to interventions to change health care provider practice [14]. Adaptations to CFIR have been made since it was first introduced, [14] but to our knowledge the model has not yet been applied to study health equity integration across health service and delivery systems. 

of the Health Equity Framework, which was viewed as a key driver for action. Greater diversity within health system leadership was also identified as an important strategy to support integration. Our findings have implications for other jurisdictions seeking to advance health equity across health service and delivery systems.

Title: A Scoping Review of Implemented Innovations in Cancer Care: Implications for Pan-Canadian Scaling
Snippet: Applying the CFIR lens to the analysis enabled grouping of cancer care innovations by key implementation domains, highlighting cross-cutting barriers, facilitators, and contextual factors influencing adoption and scale-up. Table 7 presents the identified initiatives organized according to the CFIR domains, outlining key findings, illustrative examples, barriers, and facilitators for each domain. Within organizations (Inner Setting), supportive leadership and alignment with provincial cancer strategies facilitated adoption, though resistance to role expansion and unclear definitions posed challenges. Workforce capabilities (Characteristics of Individuals) emerged as a pivotal factor, with digital literacy and access to specialized training influencing readiness for AI-enabled tools, virtual platforms, and expanded scope-of-practice roles. Implementation processes that incorporated early stakeholder engagement, multi-sectoral collaboration, and embedded evaluation (Process) were associated with more successful and sustainable scale-ups. However, persistent barriers, including regulatory variability, infrastructure gaps, inconsistent funding, and limited Canadian-based training, highlight the importance of coordinated pan-Canadian policy action to sustain and expand these innovations [15,16]. Table 7 presents the synthesis of findings mapped to CFIR domains. The framework was applied during evidence integration and interpretation to identify recurring implementation determinants across the literature, grey literature, survey, and interview findings and to examine factors influencing the adoption, sustainability, and scale of cancer care innovations.

documents.snippet:
The ways that health equity is integrated into the different components of the health service and delivery system can be better understood through the lens of Implementation Science (IS). IS has been defined as the study of methods to promote the adoption and integration of evidence-based health interventions (e.g., tools, programs, and policies) into practice [12]. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) is a commonly used IS framework that can guide the systematic assessment of multi-level implementation contexts to identify or explain barriers and facilitators that might influence intervention implementation and effectiveness [13]. The CFIR is comprised of 39 constructs that operate across five domains (Innovation, Outer Setting, Inner Setting, Individuals, and Process) [13]. The CFIR has been applied to a range of contexts within health systems, ranging from individual programs to improve service delivery, to interventions to change health care provider practice [14]. Adaptations to CFIR have been made since it was first introduced, [14] but to our knowledge the model has not yet been applied to study health equity integration across health service and delivery systems.

Title: Ambidextrous IT Governance Enactment in Healthcare: A Comparison between the Swedish and Ugandan Setting
Snippet: The digitalization of society is ushering in new directions for organizations and individuals alike. Core to the notion of digitalization is the parallel utilization of digital technologies for increased efficiency and increased innovation, with new operating models introduced in parallel with continuous enhancements of efficiency [1,2]. Within healthcare, notions such as Healthcare IT (HIT) and e-health initiatives have a long tradition [3,4], and the development is expected to continue [5]. With the increased digitalization of healthcare, new challenges emerge concerning how technology should be organized, managed and governed [2,6]. In order to support the digitalization of healthcare, it is imperative that we have the right IT governance mechanisms in place. 

The extant literature has identified IT Governance as a pre-requisite for not only organizational success, but also effective, continued digitalization [9]. In this vein, IT Governance refers to decision rights and accountability framework for encouraging desirable behaviours in the use of IT [8], further explicated as a combination of processes, structures and relational mechanisms. 

Traditional IT Governance has, however, been criticized for a tendency of bureaucratization and IT function myopia [10], as well as not amply addressing the organization's parallel needs for efficiency and innovation [11]. This need has been studied within the literature concerning organizational ambidexterity, here understood in line with [12] & [13] as the parallel attainment of exploitation and exploration. Resource orchestration [30] is an emerging stream that has the potential to extend the understanding of resource-based theory (RBT) by explicitly addressing the role of managers' actions to effectively structure, bundle, and leverage organization resources. 

Recent additions to this stream of research have called for an increasing dynamic perspective to ambidexterity, i.e. that it is not a stable, fixed state but a continuous configuration of balancing [14,15]. From the dynamic perspective, IT Governance in healthcare needs to move away from only having the senior managers make the key decisions and designing organizational solutions to also empowering the operational managers so as to involve them in the development of ambidextrous strategies, i.e. designed with the intent of dynamically balancing exploitation and exploration.

Title: Transforming Hospital Administration In 2026: A Literature Review On Innovation, Efficiency, And Patient-Centered Leadership
Snippet: The study purpose was to explore how innovation, operational efficiency, and patient-centered leadership collectively shape hospital administration in 2026. The global healthcare landscape is undergoing rapid transformation, driven by digital technologies, data analytics, and evolving patient expectations. This literature review examines how hospital administrators are integrating technological advancement with adaptive leadership to improve organizational performance and patient outcomes. The review focuses on identifying key strategies that enable healthcare institutions to balance technological efficiency with the human dimensions of care. 
Materials and methods. A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Peer-reviewed articles published between 2019 and 2026 were retrieved from databases including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Studies were included if they addressed hospital administration, innovation, efficiency, or leadership within healthcare systems. Twenty-four high-quality studies were selected for qualitative synthesis. Data were analyzed thematically across three domains: digital innovation, operational efficiency, and patient-centered leadership. 
Results. Findings revealed that digital transformation, when supported by adaptive and empathetic leadership, significantly improves hospital efficiency, staff engagement, and patient satisfaction. Integration of AI, Lean Six Sigma, and data-driven governance models led to measurable gains in workflow optimization and service quality. Leadership practices emphasizing transparency, trust, and collaboration were found to mediate the success of innovation initiatives. 
Conclusions. The transformation of hospital administration in 2026 is defined by the fusion of technology and human-centered leadership. Sustainable progress depends not only on digital tools but on leaders’ capacity to align innovation with empathy and organizational purpose. The review concludes that hospitals fostering patient-centered, adaptive leadership cultures are best positioned to thrive in an era of complex healthcare transformation.

Title: Digital Leadership and Organizational Citizenship Behavior in Healthcare Organizations: A Conceptual Perspective
Snippet: Digital hospitals fully integrated healthcare facilities that rely on digital systems for patient care, clinical decision-making, and administrative processes require leaders who can align technological investments with patient safety and quality improvement goals. Effective digital leaders in healthcare settings are responsible for guiding the implementation of electronic health records, ensuring interoperability among disparate systems, and leveraging data analytics to inform clinical and operational decisions (Putra et al., 2025). Moreover, healthcare innovation, including the adoption of AI-assisted diagnostic services, robotic surgery systems, and remote patient monitoring technologies, demands leaders who can balance the promise of technological advancement with the realities of workforce readiness and patient acceptance. 

Research demonstrates that digital leadership enhances employee empowerment, which subsequently boosts techno-work engagement and sustainability performance in the public healthcare sector (Abbas et al., 2025). Empowered healthcare employees are more likely to embrace digital innovations, take initiative in problem-solving, and contribute proactively to organizational improvements. Second, facilitating adaptation requires digital leaders to guide healthcare employees through continuous technological changes by providing adequate training, creating psychologically safe environments for experimentation, and recognizing adaptive efforts. A mixed-methods systematic review identified that healthcare leaders' digital competence experiences include the need for developing leaders' own, professionals', and patients' competence in the digitalization of healthcare, as well as the ability to act as an advocate to implement technology into practice (Laakkonen et al., 2024). Third, reducing uncertainty involves digital leaders proactively communicating digital visions, clarifying expectations regarding technology use, and mitigating the ambiguities associated with digital transformation. Leaders who provide clear guidance and consistent support help alleviate the technostress and role ambiguity that often accompany digitalization. Digital leadership facilitates a supportive work environment that encourages innovation, knowledge sharing, and collective problem-solving (Cortellazzo et al., 2019). Thus, digital leadership is fundamentally about people; empowering them to adapt and thrive amid technological change rather than merely about technological mastery. In healthcare organizations, where the ultimate goal remains high-quality patient care, digital leadership must therefore integrate human-centered values with technological capabilities to foster sustainable organizational performance.

For leadership mindsets, it contrasts pilot-phase experimentation and learning [2,5] with institutionalization-phase sustained learning and core-value cultures [4]. For governance structures, it shows pilot-phase resource autonomy and clear goals [1] versus scale-up governance coordination [13] versus institutionalization's accountability structures and policy integration [7,1]. For decision processes, it traces pilot-phase learning loops and trialability [12,4] through scale-up stakeholder engagement and embedded evaluation [10] to institutionalization's routine embedding and continuous improvement [7,3]. The 'Practical comparison across implementation phases' section explicitly organizes enablers, obstructions, and process designs across all three phases with concrete citations. The answer could more sharply distinguish *differential* effects (how the same mechanism works differently in pilot vs. scale-up vs. institutionalization) from *cumulative* effects (mechanisms that build over time). Some passages conflate these two ideas.

attempts.answer:
Summary and framing
Sustainable healthcare innovation is often discussed in two complementary but distinct frames: environmental impact (e.g., decarbonization, resource efficiency, eco-design) and institutional persistence (longevity, resilience, and sustained effectiveness under financing, policy, and population-shock pressures). Across these frames, barriers cluster at multiple levels—individual, organizational/institutional, and system/policy—yet leadership, governance, and incentive design emerge as cross-cutting levers that can bridge environmental and persistence goals in health systems. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Barriers to environmentally sustainable practices span individual knowledge/attitudes and competing demands, institutional leadership and strategy, stakeholder buy-in, and broader policy/infrastructure gaps, with enablers centered on transformational leadership, collaborative engagement, and explicit vision/strategy/roadmaps</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Institutional persistence and resilience depend on coordination, accountability, and collaborative leadership that improves adaptability, trust, and innovation capacity</cite>, while <cite id="10ebd1ef-3">weak governance, fragmented policies, and unstable financing signal deeper structural vulnerabilities that undermine long-term effectiveness and equity</cite>.

Environmental-impact operationalization: barriers and enabling mechanisms
Environmental sustainability in healthcare is constrained by sectoral emissions intensity and the leverage points available to facilities. <cite id="bc9f02c5-0">Health systems contribute roughly 8–10% of U.S. emissions and up to 25% of public sector emissions in the UK, with 46% of that footprint from direct activities and 54% from supply chains; hospital interventions target both direct and indirect emissions while improving efficiency and quality</cite>. <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">Even with national roadmaps (e.g., NHS), implementation barriers remain pronounced in emerging economies, including reliance on fossil-fuel electricity, limited renewable uptake, suboptimal waste management, and uneven infrastructure, despite demonstrated emission reductions from technologies like rooftop PV and high-efficiency HVAC</cite>. 

At the organizational level, barriers include technical complexity, insufficient funding and workforce shortages, and fragmented incentives, while leadership commitment and resource allocation are repeatedly identified as enablers. <cite id="bc9f02c5-2">German hospital reviews report potential for energy efficiency, renewables, and waste reduction but note that workforce shortages, insufficient funding, and technical complexity hinder implementation; leadership commitment, resource allocation, and staff engagement are key to overcoming these barriers</cite>. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">A scoping review similarly finds individual-level barriers (time, knowledge, competing priorities and climate skepticism), institutional barriers (lack of leadership/strategy, misaligned incentives, and stakeholder buy-in deficits), and system barriers (lack of enabling policies and infrastructure), with transformational leadership and cross-stakeholder collaboration as primary enablers</cite>. 

System mechanisms to make environmental innovations stick hinge on data, incentives, procurement power, and accountability. <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">Leaders can advance decarbonization by measuring and setting emissions targets, reducing energy and waste, and reporting progress; institutional mechanisms include sustainability leadership, incentive structures tied to sustainability performance, alignment with national NDCs, and leveraging procurement to drive supplier decarbonization, with accreditation tying sustainability to reaccreditation and financial incentives</cite>. <cite id="bc9f02c5-3">Technology-enabled solutions (efficient equipment, smart infrastructure, renewables, telemedicine, AI-driven analytics) can reduce emissions while maintaining care quality, but adoption depends on supportive policy frameworks and financial incentives and coordinated multi-stakeholder scaling</cite>.

Institutional persistence: barriers and mechanisms
Institutional persistence—organizational longevity, continuity of quality, and resilience against shocks—rests on effective governance, coherent financing, and people-centered service delivery. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Weak coordination, fragmented leadership, limited accountability, and sectoral fragmentation undermine responsiveness and efficiency; these governance deficits reduce implementation fidelity and innovation capacity, whereas collaborative leadership that emphasizes shared decision-making, stakeholder engagement, and cross-sector cooperation is associated with improved adaptability, communication, integrated delivery, trust, and resilience</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-1">Collaborative governance reduces barriers by facilitating interprofessional interaction and collective problem-solving, strengthening policy implementation and resilience during uncertainty; participatory leadership improves engagement, trust, and coordination, with effects particularly salient in primary care settings facing resource constraints</cite>. 

Structural vulnerabilities—fragmented financing, policy misalignment, and weak governance—erode sustainability as a marker of long-term viability and equity. <cite id="10ebd1ef-3">Systems prioritizing sustainability demonstrate resilience against economic shocks, demographic change, and crises, signaling structural maturity; persistent inequities and weak governance reveal deeper institutional/political challenges, with political commitment, strategic planning, and societal consensus as underpinnings of coherent, durable reforms</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Financing stability supports workforce retention, infrastructure, and continuity; policy fragmentation and decentralization without capacity produce uneven quality and access, while curative-oriented financing undermines long-term efficiency and sustainability; transparent, accountable governance reduces leakage and inequities, and community engagement enhances adaptability</cite>. 

A broader systems lens links governance, evidence use, workforce, and equitable innovation to resilience. <cite id="10ebd1ef-2">Strengthening health systems requires integrated, multisectoral, evidence-informed strategies connecting governance/policy, service delivery and quality, workforce well-being, and equity/innovation; translating evidence into coherent policy and implementation across levels is essential for resilient, people-centered systems</cite>. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Sustainable leadership faces systemic barriers—time/resource constraints, workforce shortages, political climate, and rigid hierarchies—yet actionable solutions include protected strategic time, leadership development, culture of psychological safety, redefining leadership metrics to include culture and innovation, technology/process streamlining, cross-sector collaboration, and data-driven decision-making</cite>.

Comparing barrier profiles across the two operationalizations
The barrier profiles differ in locus and expression but share common roots in leadership, incentives, and cross-level alignment. Environmentally focused innovations face:
- Technical and supply-chain constraints: energy intensity, 24/365 operations, dependence on grid/fossil fuels, complex equipment and waste streams. <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">Hospitals’ continuous energy demand, reliance on diesel/coal-based power, and limited waste treatment infrastructure in many countries raise per-bed emissions, while renewable adoption and efficiency upgrades can cut emissions by 20–30% in some settings</cite>.
- Organizational capacity and financing gaps: workforce shortages, insufficient funding, and technical complexity impede adoption. <cite id="bc9f02c5-2">Leadership commitment, resource allocation, and staff engagement are repeatedly cited as necessary to implement sustainability measures</cite>.
- System and policy gaps: lack of emissions data/reporting standards, misaligned incentives, and inadequate procurement/capacity to drive supplier change. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Policy and infrastructure gaps hinder transformational change; stakeholder buy-in and leadership style condition success</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">aggregating and analyzing emissions data, setting targets, public reporting, sustainability-linked incentives, and procurement power are core institutional mechanisms</cite>.

Institutional persistence faces barriers that are more governance- and viability-oriented:
- Coordination/accountability deficits and fragmented leadership that slow or distort implementation and innovation. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Weak institutional coordination, fragmented leadership structures, and limited accountability reduce responsiveness and efficiency; governance capacity is crucial amid chronic diseases, emergencies, and inequities</cite>.
- Financing and policy fragmentation undermining continuity and equity; curative bias strains budgets and trust. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Uncoordinated financing, service delivery, and governance yield implementation gaps; stable public financing supports workforce and infrastructure; curative-focused systems raise long-term costs and undermine sustainability</cite>.
- Governance opacity and weak community engagement that erode trust and adaptive capacity. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Transparent, accountable institutions improve resource allocation; poor governance correlates with service leakage and inequitable access; community engagement enhances resilience</cite>.

Convergence emerges when mapping barriers to both definitions: rigid hierarchies and siloed governance inhibit both green-tech adoption and resilient service delivery; leadership skill gaps and time/resource constraints hinder both environmental and persistence-oriented innovation; and misaligned incentives and fragmented policies stall cross-level coordination. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Leaders report struggling to balance daily operations with strategy, with outdated hierarchical decision-making stifling innovation and adaptability</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">institutional barriers like lack of strategy and incentives similarly obstruct environmental change</cite>; <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">fragmented governance undermines responsiveness and innovation capacity, weakening resilience</cite>.

Do governance and leadership mechanisms generalize across definitions?
Cross-cutting mechanisms align across environmental and persistence frames when they target leadership quality, governance architecture, incentives, and system alignment. Leadership and governance:
- Collaborative, evidence-informed, shared decision-making improves adaptability, innovation capacity, and resilience, enabling both green innovations and durable service delivery. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Collaborative leadership—shared decision-making, stakeholder engagement, cross-sector cooperation—enhances adaptability, communication, and resilience, improving institutional effectiveness and trust</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">transformational leadership that prioritizes engagement across stakeholders is a primary enabler of environmental change</cite>.
- Strategic planning and accountability structures (vision, targets, monitoring, and accreditation) bridge both domains. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Effective strategies specify vision, targets, incentives, and stakeholder roles and roadmaps that ensure time for quality care while achieving targets</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">accreditation tied to sustainability performance and reaccreditation, plus incentive alignment with national NDCs, institutionalizes accountability for decarbonization</cite>.
- Workforce capability and culture: leadership development, protected time, psychological safety, and ethical, transparent cultures sustain both environmental change and long-term organizational resilience. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Protected strategic time, leadership training/mentorship, psychological safety and innovation-oriented metrics, cross-sector collaboration, and technology to streamline leadership roles are actionable solutions for sustainable leadership</cite>.

Financing and policy integration:
- Aligning budgets, incentives, and risk pooling supports both environmental and persistence goals by stabilizing resources for people and infrastructure and rewarding resilience. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Risk pooling and cross-subsidization reduce household financial vulnerability and reinforce trust; stable public financing supports workforce retention and continuity</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">sustainability-linked incentives and public reporting internalize environmental performance into operations and accreditation</cite>.
- Decoupling perverse incentives and correcting governance fragmentation improve implementation fidelity and equity. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Policy fragmentation and weak governance reduce efficiency and exacerbate disparities; transparent institutions curb leakage</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">clarifying incentives and stakeholder buy-in at the institutional level accelerates environmental practice adoption</cite>.

Integrative frameworks (SDGs/UHC) clarify that environmental and persistence-oriented sustainability are mutually reinforcing. <cite id="10ebd1ef-2">Achieving UHC and the SDGs requires resilient, evidence-informed, people-centered systems that integrate governance, service quality, workforce, and equitable innovation</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-3">Sustainability functions as an early indicator of long-term UHC success; systems prioritizing sustainability show resilience against shocks and reduce inequities</cite>. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Environmental practice implementation benefits when guided by stakeholder-inclusive strategies, targets, and monitoring, echoing governance principles that sustain institutional effectiveness</cite>.

Practical integration: designing mechanisms that work across definitions
- Co-locate environmental and longevity goals in joint roadmaps: define sector emissions targets aligned to NDCs and UHC milestones; allocate protected time and budgets for cross-departmental sustainability leadership; and embed environmental KPIs into operational and financial oversight. <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">Set emissions targets, reduce energy/waste, report progress, tie sustainability to reaccreditation and financial incentives, and leverage procurement to drive supplier change</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">roadmaps should specify vision, targets, incentives, stakeholder roles, and ensure clinicians have time to maintain quality</cite>.
- Build governance coalitions: convene clinical, finance, sustainability, supply chain, and community stakeholders to sequence changes (e.g., procurement and energy first where leverage is high), resolve cross-departmental incentives, and share decision-making. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Collaborative leadership across sectors strengthens coordination, trust, and innovation capacity</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">stakeholder buy-in and collaborative governance are primary enablers</cite>.
- Invest in workforce capability and culture: leadership training, psychological safety for proposing low-carbon alternatives, and transparent ethical governance to sustain adoption. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Structured leadership support, protected time, and culture change toward innovation and wellbeing improve sustainable leadership performance</cite>.
- Sequence and pilot innovations: prioritize low-regret, high-leverage levers (e.g., energy efficiency, procurement, waste segregation) while using pilots to build evidence and stakeholder trust; couple with financing reforms (risk pooling, cross-subsidies) to stabilize resources. <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">Rooftop solar and HVAC upgrades achieved 20–30% emission reductions with cost savings; waste segregation reduced incineration dependence</cite>; <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">risk pooling and cross-subsidization stabilize financing and protect households</cite>.

Caveats and context
Context matters: hospitals in high-income settings face different procurement and grid-access constraints than those in emerging economies, where financing and infrastructure gaps are acute. <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">Supply chain emissions dominate sector footprints, requiring procurement power and insurance/financing instruments</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">developing countries confront fossil-dominant electricity, limited renewables, and uneven waste infrastructure</cite>. Governance quality mediates whether policy commitments translate into practice; leadership style and institutional capacity determine whether environmental gains institutionalize into resilience. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Hierarchical, fragmented governance limits responsiveness and innovation capacity, whereas collaborative leadership improves adaptability and resilience</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">institutions lacking leadership, incentives, and stakeholder buy-in struggle to sustain environmental practices</cite>.

Conclusion
When sustainability is operationalized as environmental impact, barriers concentrate on technical, supply-chain, and organizational capacity constraints, mitigated by data-driven targets, procurement leverage, leadership commitment, and accreditation-linked incentives. When operationalized as institutional persistence, barriers center on governance fragmentation, financing instability, and weak accountability, countered by collaborative, evidence-informed leadership, coordinated policy/financing reforms, and people-centered implementation. Governance and leadership mechanisms do generalize across definitions—sustainability leadership, collaborative governance, strategic roadmapping with targets and incentives, workforce capability building, and cross-sector coalitions are cross-cutting enablers that can integrate environmental improvements with durable organizational resilience—yet their effectiveness depends on context-specific tailoring and strong alignment between policy, financing, and clinical operations. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Leadership, stakeholder engagement, strategy, targets, incentives, and roadmaps enable environmental practice adoption</cite> <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">sustainability leadership, incentives, and accreditation/reporting institutionalize decarbonization</cite> <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">collaborative leadership enhances adaptability, trust, and resilience</cite> <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">coherent financing, transparent governance, and community engagement underpin durable, equitable performance</cite>.

Title: Empowering Sustainable Healthcare: The Role of Health Literacy
Snippet: HL might be key for sustainable healthcare; however, numerous barriers limit its advancement and, consequently, the realization of sustainability in healthcare services and systems. The identification of facilitators and barriers in HL development is crucial for crafting effective interventions. Perhaps the most significant barrier is that HL is a relatively new concept, which impacts various aspects in different ways. Particularly, the evidence required to drive stakeholder decision-making processes, as described above, is highly heterogeneous, inadequately addressed systematically, and still lacking in some fields, therefore limiting its generalizability and applicability [95]. Furthermore, outside the academic environment, the concept of HL is not as widely recognized as it should be [39]. The collaboration between academia, healthcare institutions, and community organizations is a path to follow for the implementation of HL promoting interventions. By overcoming these barriers, we can also enhance the role of HL in building sustainable healthcare practices and improving health outcomes for all. Understanding these dynamics provides insights into how HL can be nurtured and sustained over time, highlighting the importance of longitudinal and multifaceted approaches to HL enhancement [96]. Title: Perceptions of Sustainable Leadership in Australian Healthcare
Snippet: Purpose Sustainable leadership is essential for addressing workforce shortages, technological advancements, and increasing regulatory demands in Australian healthcare. Many healthcare leaders assume their roles based on clinical expertise rather than formal leadership training, highlighting the need for structured support. This study explores sustainable leadership in Australian healthcare, identifying key challenges, support mechanisms, and strategies for improvement. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 276 managers, leaders, and supervisors working in Australian healthcare organisations. Participants were recruited through professional networks, social media, and direct invitations. The survey, administered via Qualtrics, examined leadership training, characteristics of sustainable leadership, challenges, and available support systems. Quantitative data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics, while qualitative responses underwent thematic analysis. Results Leadership training was primarily informal, with limited access to structured programs due to time and financial constraints. Sustainable leadership was defined as balancing operational demands with long-term planning, ethical decision-making, and fostering a resilient workplace culture. Key challenges included staff retention, change management, and hierarchical structures limiting innovation. Support for leaders was inconsistent, with male leaders reporting higher perceived support. Systemic barriers, such as outdated leadership models and a focus on financial performance over workplace culture, restricted sustainable leadership implementation. Conclusion To enhance sustainable leadership, organisations must prioritize structured training, mentorship, and inclusive leadership pathways. Addressing systemic barriers and redefining leadership success beyond financial metrics will strengthen leadership resilience, reduce burnout, and improve healthcare outcomes.

They also pointed to the critical role of ethical decision-making, transparency, and trust in boosting team morale and reducing burnout. However, despite recognising its importance, participants lowly rated the sustainability of healthcare leadership. As Gerard et al 29 suggest, leadership must go beyond achieving operational goals to nurture an inclusive and supportive culture that prioritises staff well-being, fosters innovation, and encourages professional development. This gap between theory and practice underscores the pressing need for strategies that make sustainable leadership a reality across healthcare organisations. Embedding these principles into daily leadership practices will not only address current challenges but also build a foundation for resilience and excellence in the future.

Title: Bridging health and global climate policy: Opportunities for policymakers and health systems
Snippet: Health systems leaders can advance decarbonization by aggregating and analyzing emissions data annually, setting emissions targets, reducing energy use and waste, and publicly reporting on progress for their own environmental footprint [28]. Institutional mechanisms should include sustainability leadership, incentive structures tied to sustainability progress [29], and alignment with national NDC targets to ensure transparency and enable sectoral progress tracking. Since supply chain activities account for over 80 % of total emissions, transitioning to sustainable procurement and operations is essential [30,29]. By integrating sustainability criteria into purchasing decisions, the healthcare sector can leverage their significant market power to influence suppliers to adopt lower-emission practices. In doing so, the healthcare sector can set a benchmark for adjacent industries like manufacturing, transportation, and energy to follow [31]. Insurance can further accelerate this shift by incentivizing low-emission practices and climate-conscious programs, as Medicare and Medicaid have already begun piloting in the US [32]. 

Several countries offer lessons for decarbonization strategies. In the United States (U.S.), more than 1200 hospitalsrepresenting over 19 % of U.S. hospitalshave signed the Health Sector Climate Pledge, committing to reducing emissions 50 % by 2030 and achieving net zero emissions by 2050 [33]. These institutions pledge to publish annual progress, conduct supply chain emissions inventories, and develop resilience plans for vulnerable communities. In the United Kingdom (U. K.), the National Health Service (NHS) has committed to becoming the world's first net-zero health system, supported by emissions tracking, green procurement policies, and carbon literacy training for clinical staff. 

Accreditation bodies can play a critical role in scaling health sector decarbonization. To ensure lasting impact, decarbonization progress should be incorporated into the Joint Commission's reaccreditation process. In the U.K., the NHS has tied carbon performance to financial and operational incentives. Embedding sustainability metrics into accreditation frameworks can institutionalize long-term accountability and align healthcare operations with national climate commitments and NDC goals.

Title: Decarbonizing Indonesian hospitals challenges and causal pathways toward sustainable healthcare
Snippet: Healthcare facilities, particularly hospitals, are recognized for their intensive resource consumption and environmental footprint. Operating 24 h a day, hospitals require substantial energy to support medical equipment, HVAC systems, lighting, and sterilization processes. Cristiano et al. [10] and Sanyal et al. [43] indicate that the healthcare sector contributes approximately 4.4% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, making it a significant environmental concern. For example, the United Kingdom's National Health Service (NHS) has identified hospital operations as a major emission source and has introduced a nationwide net-zero roadmap, resulting in measurable reductions in energy-related emissions [5]. 

In developing countries like Indonesia, the situation is exacerbated by limited adoption of renewable energy, suboptimal waste management practices, and reliance on fossil-fuel-based energy sources [3]. National energy profiles show that hospitals remain highly dependent on fossil-fuel-based electricity and diesel generators, while modern waste treatment infrastructure is unevenly distributed across regions. Similar conditions have been reported in public hospitals in India and Southeast Asia, where reliance on carbon-intensive energy systems leads to higher per-bed emissions compared to hospitals in high-income countries. 

Hospital decarbonizing refers to the systematic reduction of carbon emissions across healthcare operations, including energy use, waste management, medical equipment, and procurement (H. [45]). Key strategies include transitioning to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, optimizing waste handling, and integrating environmentally friendly medical technologies. Empirical evidence from Germany shows that hospitals adopting rooftop solar photovoltaic systems and high-efficiency HVAC technologies have achieved emission reductions of 20-30% alongside long-term cost savings. Likewise, hospitals in Japan have implemented advanced waste segregation and recycling systems, significantly reducing dependence on carbon-intensive incineration. 

At the global level, initiatives such as the Global Green and Healthy Hospitals (GGHH) Agenda promote low-carbon healthcare systems through sustainable infrastructure, procurement, and climate-resilient operations. Hospitals participating in the GGHH network in Germany and Australia have reported improvements in energy performance and waste reduction, while also strengthening organizational awareness of sustainability practices [44]. Despite these successes, implementation remains uneven, particularly in emerging economies. 

Numerous barriers continue to impede hospital decarbonization efforts.

Title: Strengthening health system governance through collaborative leadership to improve primary healthcare effectiveness
Snippet: Primary healthcare remains the cornerstone of equitable health systems and universal health coverage in many countries, particularly in low-and middle-income settings where healthcare resources are unevenly distributed [1]. Despite ongoing reforms in healthcare administration and financing, the effectiveness of primary healthcare services continues to be hampered by major governance challenges. Weak institutional coordination, fragmented leadership structures, limited accountability mechanisms, and inadequate collaboration among stakeholders frequently reduce the responsiveness and efficiency of healthcare delivery systems [2]. In many regions, health facilities operate within complex organizational environments that require coordinated decision-making between health professionals, local governments, community organizations, and policymakers [3]. However, governance processes often remain hierarchical and sectorally fragmented, limiting primary healthcare systems' ability to respond adaptively to population health needs [4]. 

The governance capacity of health systems has become increasingly important following the growing burden of chronic diseases, public health emergencies, and healthcare inequities [5]. Previous evidence has demonstrated that ineffective governance contributes to poor healthcare accessibility, inefficient resource allocation, low community trust, and suboptimal service integration [6]. Studies conducted in several developing countries have shown that leadership limitations within healthcare organizations frequently lead to delayed policy implementation, inconsistent health service standards, and weak institutional accountability [7]. In primary healthcare settings, leadership practices influence not only administrative performance but also interdisciplinary collaboration, workforce motivation, and community participation. Consequently, strengthening governance mechanisms has emerged as a strategic priority for improving healthcare system performance and sustainability [8]. 

Collaborative leadership has recently gained attention as an alternative governance approach capable of addressing organizational complexity in healthcare systems [9]. Unlike conventional hierarchical leadership models, collaborative leadership emphasizes shared decision-making, collective responsibility, stakeholder engagement, and cross-sectoral cooperation [10]. This leadership approach encourages healthcare managers, practitioners, local authorities, and community representatives to jointly participate in policy formulation and problem-solving in healthcare [11]. Existing studies have indicated that collaborative leadership may improve organizational adaptability, strengthen communication among healthcare actors, and support integrated service delivery [12]. Evidence from hospital and public health management research suggests that collaborative governance models are associated with improved institutional trust, greater innovation capacity, and stronger organizational resilience [13]. 

Several empirical studies have also highlighted the relationship between collaborative leadership and healthcare effectiveness.
</snippet>

Title: Strengthening health system governance through collaborative leadership to improve primary healthcare effectiveness
Snippet: Collaborative leadership may reduce these barriers by facilitating interprofessional interaction and promoting collective problem-solving among healthcare personnel [27]. Through collaborative governance processes, healthcare institutions may become more adaptive to local health priorities and more capable of responding efficiently to community healthcare needs [28]. 

The findings of this study are generally consistent with previous research emphasizing the importance of collaborative governance within healthcare organizations. Several earlier studies reported that participatory leadership approaches improved workforce engagement, institutional trust, and healthcare coordination [29]. Research conducted in community health programs and public health institutions also demonstrated that collaborative leadership strengthened policy implementation and enhanced organizational resilience during periods of healthcare uncertainty. Similar findings have been observed in studies examining integrated healthcare systems, where leadership collaboration was associated with improved communication and more efficient resource management. 

However, the present study extends previous literature in several important ways. First, much of the earlier research focused predominantly on hospital administration or organizational culture, while limited empirical evidence has examined collaborative leadership specifically within primary healthcare governance systems. Primary healthcare settings differ substantially from tertiary healthcare institutions because they operate closer to community populations and often face greater resource limitations, workforce shortages, and administrative fragmentation. By focusing on primary healthcare governance, this study contributes a more contextually relevant understanding of how collaborative leadership operates within frontline healthcare systems. 

Second, this study highlights the interconnectedness of leadership, governance, and healthcare effectiveness in decentralized healthcare environments. Existing literature frequently treats leadership competencies and governance quality as separate organizational constructs, whereas present findings demonstrate that these dimensions are structurally interconnected. Collaborative leadership may strengthen governance processes by improving stakeholder coordination, enhancing institutional participation, and promoting collective accountability. Consequently, healthcare effectiveness should not be interpreted solely as an operational outcome, but also as a reflection of governance quality and institutional collaboration. 

The study additionally contributes to broader conceptual discussions regarding health system governance in developing countries. Many healthcare reforms in low-and middle-income countries continue to emphasize administrative restructuring and financing expansion while paying relatively limited attention to collaborative governance processes. The findings suggest that governance effectiveness may depend not only on policy design or organizational resources but also on the quality of leadership interaction and institutional cooperation within healthcare systems. Strengthening collaborative leadership capacities may therefore represent a practical strategy for improving healthcare system resilience, particularly in settings characterized by limited resources and complex administrative arrangements. 

Despite these contributions, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.
</snippet>

Title: FROM POLICY TO PRACTICE: STRENGTHENING HEALTH SYSTEMS THROUGH EVIDENCE, EQUITY, AND INNOVATION
Snippet: Health systems worldwide are confronting increasingly complex challenges driven by demographic and epidemiological shifts transitions, technological advance, emerging health threats. Achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) therefore requires health systems that are not only accessible but also resilient, evidence-informed, and people-centered. This editorial synthesizes the contributions of the studies published in this issue through four interconnected dimensions of health system strengthening: governance and policy, service delivery and quality, the health workforce, and equity and innovation. The articles demonstrate that effective governance depends on translating evidence into coherent policies and successful implementation across different levels of the health system. High-quality service delivery requires organizational readiness, patient-centered care, and continuous quality improvement, while a resilient health workforce relies on supportive leadership, workforce well-being, and enabling work environments. The studies further highlight the importance of addressing social and geographic inequities and ensuring that technological innovations are implemented equitably to improve health outcomes across diverse populations. Together, these contributions reinforce the need for integrated, multisectoral, and evidence-informed strategies that connect governance, service delivery, workforce development, and equitable innovation. Strengthening these interconnected components is essential for building resilient health systems capable of responding to current challenges. 
Keyword: health systems, Universal Health Coverage, health policy.

Summary and framing
Sustainable healthcare innovation is often discussed in two complementary but distinct frames: environmental impact (e.g., decarbonization, resource efficiency, eco-design) and institutional persistence (longevity, resilience, and sustained effectiveness under financing, policy, and population-shock pressures). Across these frames, barriers cluster at multiple levels—individual, organizational/institutional, and system/policy—yet leadership, governance, and incentive design emerge as cross-cutting levers that can bridge environmental and persistence goals in health systems. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Barriers to environmentally sustainable practices span individual knowledge/attitudes and competing demands, institutional leadership and strategy, stakeholder buy-in, and broader policy/infrastructure gaps, with enablers centered on transformational leadership, collaborative engagement, and explicit vision/strategy/roadmaps</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Institutional persistence and resilience depend on coordination, accountability, and collaborative leadership that improves adaptability, trust, and innovation capacity</cite>, while <cite id="10ebd1ef-3">weak governance, fragmented policies, and unstable financing signal deeper structural vulnerabilities that undermine long-term effectiveness and equity</cite>.

Environmental-impact operationalization: barriers and enabling mechanisms
Environmental sustainability in healthcare is constrained by sectoral emissions intensity and the leverage points available to facilities. <cite id="bc9f02c5-0">Health systems contribute roughly 8–10% of U.S. emissions and up to 25% of public sector emissions in the UK, with 46% of that footprint from direct activities and 54% from supply chains; hospital interventions target both direct and indirect emissions while improving efficiency and quality</cite>. <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">Even with national roadmaps (e.g., NHS), implementation barriers remain pronounced in emerging economies, including reliance on fossil-fuel electricity, limited renewable uptake, suboptimal waste management, and uneven infrastructure, despite demonstrated emission reductions from technologies like rooftop PV and high-efficiency HVAC</cite>. 

At the organizational level, barriers include technical complexity, insufficient funding and workforce shortages, and fragmented incentives, while leadership commitment and resource allocation are repeatedly identified as enablers. <cite id="bc9f02c5-2">German hospital reviews report potential for energy efficiency, renewables, and waste reduction but note that workforce shortages, insufficient funding, and technical complexity hinder implementation; leadership commitment, resource allocation, and staff engagement are key to overcoming these barriers</cite>. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">A scoping review similarly finds individual-level barriers (time, knowledge, competing priorities and climate skepticism), institutional barriers (lack of leadership/strategy, misaligned incentives, and stakeholder buy-in deficits), and system barriers (lack of enabling policies and infrastructure), with transformational leadership and cross-stakeholder collaboration as primary enablers</cite>. 

System mechanisms to make environmental innovations stick hinge on data, incentives, procurement power, and accountability. <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">Leaders can advance decarbonization by measuring and setting emissions targets, reducing energy and waste, and reporting progress; institutional mechanisms include sustainability leadership, incentive structures tied to sustainability performance, alignment with national NDCs, and leveraging procurement to drive supplier decarbonization, with accreditation tying sustainability to reaccreditation and financial incentives</cite>. <cite id="bc9f02c5-3">Technology-enabled solutions (efficient equipment, smart infrastructure, renewables, telemedicine, AI-driven analytics) can reduce emissions while maintaining care quality, but adoption depends on supportive policy frameworks and financial incentives and coordinated multi-stakeholder scaling</cite>.

Institutional persistence: barriers and mechanisms
Institutional persistence—organizational longevity, continuity of quality, and resilience against shocks—rests on effective governance, coherent financing, and people-centered service delivery. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Weak coordination, fragmented leadership, limited accountability, and sectoral fragmentation undermine responsiveness and efficiency; these governance deficits reduce implementation fidelity and innovation capacity, whereas collaborative leadership that emphasizes shared decision-making, stakeholder engagement, and cross-sector cooperation is associated with improved adaptability, communication, integrated delivery, trust, and resilience</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-1">Collaborative governance reduces barriers by facilitating interprofessional interaction and collective problem-solving, strengthening policy implementation and resilience during uncertainty; participatory leadership improves engagement, trust, and coordination, with effects particularly salient in primary care settings facing resource constraints</cite>. 

Structural vulnerabilities—fragmented financing, policy misalignment, and weak governance—erode sustainability as a marker of long-term viability and equity. <cite id="10ebd1ef-3">Systems prioritizing sustainability demonstrate resilience against economic shocks, demographic change, and crises, signaling structural maturity; persistent inequities and weak governance reveal deeper institutional/political challenges, with political commitment, strategic planning, and societal consensus as underpinnings of coherent, durable reforms</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Financing stability supports workforce retention, infrastructure, and continuity; policy fragmentation and decentralization without capacity produce uneven quality and access, while curative-oriented financing undermines long-term efficiency and sustainability; transparent, accountable governance reduces leakage and inequities, and community engagement enhances adaptability</cite>. 

A broader systems lens links governance, evidence use, workforce, and equitable innovation to resilience. <cite id="10ebd1ef-2">Strengthening health systems requires integrated, multisectoral, evidence-informed strategies connecting governance/policy, service delivery and quality, workforce well-being, and equity/innovation; translating evidence into coherent policy and implementation across levels is essential for resilient, people-centered systems</cite>. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Sustainable leadership faces systemic barriers—time/resource constraints, workforce shortages, political climate, and rigid hierarchies—yet actionable solutions include protected strategic time, leadership development, culture of psychological safety, redefining leadership metrics to include culture and innovation, technology/process streamlining, cross-sector collaboration, and data-driven decision-making</cite>.

Comparing barrier profiles across the two operationalizations
The barrier profiles differ in locus and expression but share common roots in leadership, incentives, and cross-level alignment. Environmentally focused innovations face:
- Technical and supply-chain constraints: energy intensity, 24/365 operations, dependence on grid/fossil fuels, complex equipment and waste streams. <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">Hospitals’ continuous energy demand, reliance on diesel/coal-based power, and limited waste treatment infrastructure in many countries raise per-bed emissions, while renewable adoption and efficiency upgrades can cut emissions by 20–30% in some settings</cite>.
- Organizational capacity and financing gaps: workforce shortages, insufficient funding, and technical complexity impede adoption. <cite id="bc9f02c5-2">Leadership commitment, resource allocation, and staff engagement are repeatedly cited as necessary to implement sustainability measures</cite>.
- System and policy gaps: lack of emissions data/reporting standards, misaligned incentives, and inadequate procurement/capacity to drive supplier change. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Policy and infrastructure gaps hinder transformational change; stakeholder buy-in and leadership style condition success</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">aggregating and analyzing emissions data, setting targets, public reporting, sustainability-linked incentives, and procurement power are core institutional mechanisms</cite>.

Institutional persistence faces barriers that are more governance- and viability-oriented:
- Coordination/accountability deficits and fragmented leadership that slow or distort implementation and innovation. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Weak institutional coordination, fragmented leadership structures, and limited accountability reduce responsiveness and efficiency; governance capacity is crucial amid chronic diseases, emergencies, and inequities</cite>.
- Financing and policy fragmentation undermining continuity and equity; curative bias strains budgets and trust. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Uncoordinated financing, service delivery, and governance yield implementation gaps; stable public financing supports workforce and infrastructure; curative-focused systems raise long-term costs and undermine sustainability</cite>.
- Governance opacity and weak community engagement that erode trust and adaptive capacity. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Transparent, accountable institutions improve resource allocation; poor governance correlates with service leakage and inequitable access; community engagement enhances resilience</cite>.

Convergence emerges when mapping barriers to both definitions: rigid hierarchies and siloed governance inhibit both green-tech adoption and resilient service delivery; leadership skill gaps and time/resource constraints hinder both environmental and persistence-oriented innovation; and misaligned incentives and fragmented policies stall cross-level coordination. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Leaders report struggling to balance daily operations with strategy, with outdated hierarchical decision-making stifling innovation and adaptability</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">institutional barriers like lack of strategy and incentives similarly obstruct environmental change</cite>; <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">fragmented governance undermines responsiveness and innovation capacity, weakening resilience</cite>.

Do governance and leadership mechanisms generalize across definitions?
Cross-cutting mechanisms align across environmental and persistence frames when they target leadership quality, governance architecture, incentives, and system alignment. Leadership and governance:
- Collaborative, evidence-informed, shared decision-making improves adaptability, innovation capacity, and resilience, enabling both green innovations and durable service delivery. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Collaborative leadership—shared decision-making, stakeholder engagement, cross-sector cooperation—enhances adaptability, communication, and resilience, improving institutional effectiveness and trust</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">transformational leadership that prioritizes engagement across stakeholders is a primary enabler of environmental change</cite>.
- Strategic planning and accountability structures (vision, targets, monitoring, and accreditation) bridge both domains. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Effective strategies specify vision, targets, incentives, and stakeholder roles and roadmaps that ensure time for quality care while achieving targets</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">accreditation tied to sustainability performance and reaccreditation, plus incentive alignment with national NDCs, institutionalizes accountability for decarbonization</cite>.
- Workforce capability and culture: leadership development, protected time, psychological safety, and ethical, transparent cultures sustain both environmental change and long-term organizational resilience. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Protected strategic time, leadership training/mentorship, psychological safety and innovation-oriented metrics, cross-sector collaboration, and technology to streamline leadership roles are actionable solutions for sustainable leadership</cite>.

Financing and policy integration:
- Aligning budgets, incentives, and risk pooling supports both environmental and persistence goals by stabilizing resources for people and infrastructure and rewarding resilience. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Risk pooling and cross-subsidization reduce household financial vulnerability and reinforce trust; stable public financing supports workforce retention and continuity</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">sustainability-linked incentives and public reporting internalize environmental performance into operations and accreditation</cite>.
- Decoupling perverse incentives and correcting governance fragmentation improve implementation fidelity and equity. <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">Policy fragmentation and weak governance reduce efficiency and exacerbate disparities; transparent institutions curb leakage</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">clarifying incentives and stakeholder buy-in at the institutional level accelerates environmental practice adoption</cite>.

Integrative frameworks (SDGs/UHC) clarify that environmental and persistence-oriented sustainability are mutually reinforcing. <cite id="10ebd1ef-2">Achieving UHC and the SDGs requires resilient, evidence-informed, people-centered systems that integrate governance, service quality, workforce, and equitable innovation</cite>. <cite id="10ebd1ef-3">Sustainability functions as an early indicator of long-term UHC success; systems prioritizing sustainability show resilience against shocks and reduce inequities</cite>. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Environmental practice implementation benefits when guided by stakeholder-inclusive strategies, targets, and monitoring, echoing governance principles that sustain institutional effectiveness</cite>.

Practical integration: designing mechanisms that work across definitions
- Co-locate environmental and longevity goals in joint roadmaps: define sector emissions targets aligned to NDCs and UHC milestones; allocate protected time and budgets for cross-departmental sustainability leadership; and embed environmental KPIs into operational and financial oversight. <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">Set emissions targets, reduce energy/waste, report progress, tie sustainability to reaccreditation and financial incentives, and leverage procurement to drive supplier change</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">roadmaps should specify vision, targets, incentives, stakeholder roles, and ensure clinicians have time to maintain quality</cite>.
- Build governance coalitions: convene clinical, finance, sustainability, supply chain, and community stakeholders to sequence changes (e.g., procurement and energy first where leverage is high), resolve cross-departmental incentives, and share decision-making. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Collaborative leadership across sectors strengthens coordination, trust, and innovation capacity</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">stakeholder buy-in and collaborative governance are primary enablers</cite>.
- Invest in workforce capability and culture: leadership training, psychological safety for proposing low-carbon alternatives, and transparent ethical governance to sustain adoption. <cite id="b6c2b776-0">Structured leadership support, protected time, and culture change toward innovation and wellbeing improve sustainable leadership performance</cite>.
- Sequence and pilot innovations: prioritize low-regret, high-leverage levers (e.g., energy efficiency, procurement, waste segregation) while using pilots to build evidence and stakeholder trust; couple with financing reforms (risk pooling, cross-subsidies) to stabilize resources. <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">Rooftop solar and HVAC upgrades achieved 20–30% emission reductions with cost savings; waste segregation reduced incineration dependence</cite>; <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">risk pooling and cross-subsidization stabilize financing and protect households</cite>.

Caveats and context
Context matters: hospitals in high-income settings face different procurement and grid-access constraints than those in emerging economies, where financing and infrastructure gaps are acute. <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">Supply chain emissions dominate sector footprints, requiring procurement power and insurance/financing instruments</cite>; <cite id="bc9f02c5-4">developing countries confront fossil-dominant electricity, limited renewables, and uneven waste infrastructure</cite>. Governance quality mediates whether policy commitments translate into practice; leadership style and institutional capacity determine whether environmental gains institutionalize into resilience. <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">Hierarchical, fragmented governance limits responsiveness and innovation capacity, whereas collaborative leadership improves adaptability and resilience</cite>; <cite id="b6c2b776-2">institutions lacking leadership, incentives, and stakeholder buy-in struggle to sustain environmental practices</cite>.

Conclusion
When sustainability is operationalized as environmental impact, barriers concentrate on technical, supply-chain, and organizational capacity constraints, mitigated by data-driven targets, procurement leverage, leadership commitment, and accreditation-linked incentives. When operationalized as institutional persistence, barriers center on governance fragmentation, financing instability, and weak accountability, countered by collaborative, evidence-informed leadership, coordinated policy/financing reforms, and people-centered implementation. Governance and leadership mechanisms do generalize across definitions—sustainability leadership, collaborative governance, strategic roadmapping with targets and incentives, workforce capability building, and cross-sector coalitions are cross-cutting enablers that can integrate environmental improvements with durable organizational resilience—yet their effectiveness depends on context-specific tailoring and strong alignment between policy, financing, and clinical operations. <cite id="b6c2b776-2">Leadership, stakeholder engagement, strategy, targets, incentives, and roadmaps enable environmental practice adoption</cite> <cite id="bc9f02c5-1">sustainability leadership, incentives, and accreditation/reporting institutionalize decarbonization</cite> <cite id="10ebd1ef-0">collaborative leadership enhances adaptability, trust, and resilience</cite> <cite id="10ebd1ef-4">coherent financing, transparent governance, and community engagement underpin durable, equitable performance</cite>.

Title: Perceptions of Sustainable Leadership in Australian Healthcare
Snippet: Barriers that pose challenges to achieving sustainable leadership in healthcare were also highlighted in the results of this study. Many of these barriers are rooted in systemic issues within the sector. Time constraints, limited resources, and the broader political climate were consistently flagged as major obstacles. These findings reflect the observations of William et al 3 and Moy et al, 2 who highlighted how workforce shortages and mounting operational pressures further heighten leadership challenges in healthcare. Additionally, participants pointed out that outdated leadership models and rigid hierarchical decision-making often stifle innovation and adaptability, making it even harder for leaders to navigate modern healthcare complexities. 

Despite these challenges, participants were optimistic about actionable solutions that could pave the way for more sustainable leadership. Participants suggested protected time specifically allocated for strategic planning, ensuring leaders have the space to think and act proactively rather than reactively. Participants also stressed the importance of increasing funding for leadership training and development, along with fostering workplace cultures that prioritise psychological safety, wellbeing and innovation. They also highlighted the importance of embracing technology and streamlining processes to make leadership roles more efficient and impactful. Cross-sector collaboration and data-driven decision-making were seen as essential for building stronger, more future-focused healthcare systems.
