Title: Empowering Sustainable Healthcare: The Role of Health Literacy
Snippet: HL might be key for sustainable healthcare; however, numerous barriers limit its advancement and, consequently, the realization of sustainability in healthcare services and systems. The identification of facilitators and barriers in HL development is crucial for crafting effective interventions. Table 1 delineates the various barriers faced and opportunities available for the effective implementation of HL initiatives. Perhaps the most significant barrier is that HL is a relatively new concept, which impacts various aspects in different ways. Particularly, the evidence required to drive stakeholder decision-making processes, as described above, is highly heterogeneous, inadequately addressed systematically, and still lacking in some fields, therefore limiting its generalizability and applicability [95]. Furthermore, outside the academic environment, the concept of HL is not as widely recognized as it should be [39]. Initiatives aimed at raising awareness about HL among policymakers, healthcare providers, and the general public are therefore essential; additionally, investing in research to generate more robust and standardized evidence on HL impact across different contexts is crucial. The collaboration between academia, healthcare institutions, and community organizations is a path to follow for the implementation of HL promoting interventions. By overcoming these barriers, we can also enhance the role of HL in building sustainable healthcare practices and improving health outcomes for all. Understanding these dynamics provides insights into how HL can be nurtured and sustained over time, highlighting the importance of longitudinal and multifaceted approaches to HL enhancement [96]. Additionally, the cultural diversity within populations presents both a barrier and an opportunity: It is imperative that HL initiatives are culturally sensitive and tailored to meet the unique needs of different population groups, and in fact, various national initiatives have advocated for addressing HL to promote health equity and social justice. These initiatives present opportunities for advancing HL by fostering a conducive policy environment and garnering the support of key stakeholders in healthcare and education sectors [97]. On a policy level, HL has been recognized as a foundational principle and overarching goal in health initiatives such as Healthy People 2030. By elevating the importance of HL, policy frameworks can promote sustainable healthcare practices that are not only economically viable but also environmentally and socially sustainable [98].

Title: Barriers and enablers to implementing environmentally sustainable practices in healthcare: A scoping review and proposed roadmap
Snippet: It is evident that there is an increasing interest from and need for organizations to implement environmentally sustainable practices. 17,36,37 Scaling healthcare services to improve access without considering environmental impacts may have unintended consequences for populations at large. 38 This scoping review identified some of the barriers and enablers encountered by healthcare settings when implementing environmentally sustainable practices. While most studies focused on practices in healthcare, some clinical areas namely dentistry and surgery were the most recurring focus areas. Overall, it was found that various barriers exist and are related to various levels of the organization and beyond (i.e. individual, institutional, geographical/infrastructural, political, or other).

Patients and organizations developing clinical practice guidelines also play a role in implementation success. Conversely, enablers identified in this review were primarily related to having a transformational leadership style that fostered a collaborative approach and prioritized engagement from all key stakeholders. Title: Perceptions of Sustainable Leadership in Australian Healthcare
Snippet: Purpose Sustainable leadership is essential for addressing workforce shortages, technological advancements, and increasing regulatory demands in Australian healthcare. Many healthcare leaders assume their roles based on clinical expertise rather than formal leadership training, highlighting the need for structured support. This study explores sustainable leadership in Australian healthcare, identifying key challenges, support mechanisms, and strategies for improvement. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 276 managers, leaders, and supervisors working in Australian healthcare organisations. Participants were recruited through professional networks, social media, and direct invitations. The survey, administered via Qualtrics, examined leadership training, characteristics of sustainable leadership, challenges, and available support systems. Quantitative data were analysed using IBM SPSS Statistics, while qualitative responses underwent thematic analysis. Results Leadership training was primarily informal, with limited access to structured programs due to time and financial constraints. Sustainable leadership was defined as balancing operational demands with long-term planning, ethical decision-making, and fostering a resilient workplace culture. Key challenges included staff retention, change management, and hierarchical structures limiting innovation. Support for leaders was inconsistent, with male leaders reporting higher perceived support. Systemic barriers, such as outdated leadership models and a focus on financial performance over workplace culture, restricted sustainable leadership implementation. Conclusion To enhance sustainable leadership, organisations must prioritize structured training, mentorship, and inclusive leadership pathways. Addressing systemic barriers and redefining leadership success beyond financial metrics will strengthen leadership resilience, reduce burnout, and improve healthcare outcomes.

Title: Perceptions of Sustainable Leadership in Australian Healthcare
Snippet: This study suggests the potential of sustainable leadership in addressing both the immediate challenges of running healthcare operations and the broader goal of building long-term organisational resilience in Australia's healthcare sector. 

Participants described sustainable leadership as striking a balance between managing day-to-day demands and fostering a workplace culture focused on resilience, inclusivity, and innovation. They also pointed to the critical role of ethical decision-making, transparency, and trust in boosting team morale and reducing burnout. These findings align with the perspectives of McCann and Holt 22 and Choi 28 on fostering sustainable leadership, emphasising the importance of balancing the management of immediate operational demands with the pursuit of long-term objectives, where growth is driven by ethical, adaptable, and forward-thinking strategies. 

The findings also highlight the influence of sustainable leadership in creating environments where talented healthcare professionals can thrive, contributing to higher-quality care. However, despite recognising its importance, participants lowly rated the sustainability of healthcare leadership. This points to a gap between the recognition of sustainable leadership principles and their practical implementation in the Australian healthcare system. As Gerard et al 29 suggest, leadership must go beyond achieving operational goals to nurture an inclusive and supportive culture that prioritises staff well-being, fosters innovation, and encourages professional development. This gap between theory and practice underscores the pressing need for strategies that make sustainable leadership a reality across healthcare organisations. Embedding these principles into daily leadership practices will not only address current challenges but also build a foundation for resilience and excellence in the future.

Title: Greening the future of healthcare: implementation of sustainability strategies in German hospitals and beyond—a review
Snippet: This study explores the implementation of sustainability measures within German hospitals, emphasizing their critical role in mitigating environmental impacts and promoting public health. The healthcare sector significantly contributes to global greenhouse gas emissions, necessitating urgent reforms in energy use, waste management, construction, transportation, and food systems. Key findings highlight the potential for hospitals to enhance energy efficiency, adopt renewable energy sources, and reduce waste through innovative technologies and sustainable practices. Initiatives such as green hospital designs, climate-conscious food systems, and sustainable procurement strategies are central to reducing the ecological footprint. Despite these opportunities, barriers such as workforce shortages, insufficient funding, and technical complexity hinder progress. By prioritizing sustainability, hospitals can achieve long-term economic benefits, improve patient outcomes, and foster a healthier, more resilient society.

Title: Decarbonizing Healthcare: Leveraging New Technologies for a Sustainable and Resilient Health Sector
Snippet: Abstract   The healthcare sector is a significant contributor to global greenhouse gas emissions, making it important to adopt decarbonization strategies. Transitioning to a low-carbon healthcare system is vital not only for reducing environmental impact but also for ensuring long-term sustainability and resilience in public health systems. New technologies give an innovative solution that can reduce emissions while maintaining high standards of care. Key decarbonization measures include the adoption of energy-efficient medical equipment, smart healthcare infrastructure, and renewable energy sources in healthcare. Telemedicine is another powerful tool, reducing the need for patient travel and the associated emissions from transportation, while increasing healthcare accessibility, especially in rural or underserved areas. AI-driven diagnostics and data analytics optimize healthcare delivery, reducing waste and improving resource efficiency. Hospitals and healthcare centers can further contribute to decarbonization by integrating solar power, green building technologies, and sustainable waste management practices. These innovations not only help reduce energy consumption but also improve the overall environmental footprint of healthcare facilities. To drive widespread adoption of these technologies, policy frameworks and financial incentives must support sustainable healthcare practices. Governments, healthcare providers, and industry should collaborate to scale innovative technologies that foster a decarbonized, resilient healthcare system. By aligning healthcare with climate goals, the sector can play a leading role in mitigating climate change, improving sustainability, and ensuring better health outcomes for future generations. Incorporating new technologies into healthcare is key to achieving a sustainable health sector. The healthcare industry can reduce its environmental impact, improve operational efficiency, and build resilience against climate-related health risks Speakers/Panellists Marleen Bekker Wageningen University & Research, Wageningen, Netherlands

Title: Decarbonizing Indonesian hospitals challenges and causal pathways toward sustainable healthcare
Snippet: Healthcare facilities, particularly hospitals, are recognized for their intensive resource consumption and environmental footprint. Operating 24 h a day, hospitals require substantial energy to support medical equipment, HVAC systems, lighting, and sterilization processes. Cristiano et al. [10] and Sanyal et al. [43] indicate that the healthcare sector contributes approximately 4.4% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, making it a significant environmental concern. For example, the United Kingdom's National Health Service (NHS) has identified hospital operations as a major emission source and has introduced a nationwide net-zero roadmap, resulting in measurable reductions in energy-related emissions [5]. 

In developing countries like Indonesia, the situation is exacerbated by limited adoption of renewable energy, suboptimal waste management practices, and reliance on fossil-fuel-based energy sources [3]. National energy profiles show that hospitals remain highly dependent on fossil-fuel-based electricity and diesel generators, while modern waste treatment infrastructure is unevenly distributed across regions. Similar conditions have been reported in public hospitals in India and Southeast Asia, where reliance on carbon-intensive energy systems leads to higher per-bed emissions compared to hospitals in high-income countries. 

Hospital decarbonizing refers to the systematic reduction of carbon emissions across healthcare operations, including energy use, waste management, medical equipment, and procurement (H. [45]). Key strategies include transitioning to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, optimizing waste handling, and integrating environmentally friendly medical technologies. Empirical evidence from Germany shows that hospitals adopting rooftop solar photovoltaic systems and high-efficiency HVAC technologies have achieved emission reductions of 20-30% alongside long-term cost savings. Likewise, hospitals in Japan have implemented advanced waste segregation and recycling systems, significantly reducing dependence on carbon-intensive incineration. 

At the global level, initiatives such as the Global Green and Healthy Hospitals (GGHH) Agenda promote low-carbon healthcare systems through sustainable infrastructure, procurement, and climate-resilient operations. Hospitals participating in the GGHH network in Germany and Australia have reported improvements in energy performance and waste reduction, while also strengthening organizational awareness of sustainability practices [44]. Despite these successes, implementation remains uneven, particularly in emerging economies. 

Numerous barriers continue to impede hospital decarbonization efforts.

Title: Strengthening health system governance through collaborative leadership to improve primary healthcare effectiveness
Snippet: Primary healthcare remains the cornerstone of equitable health systems and universal health coverage in many countries, particularly in low-and middle-income settings where healthcare resources are unevenly distributed [1]. Despite ongoing reforms in healthcare administration and financing, the effectiveness of primary healthcare services continues to be hampered by major governance challenges. Weak institutional coordination, fragmented leadership structures, limited accountability mechanisms, and inadequate collaboration among stakeholders frequently reduce the responsiveness and efficiency of healthcare delivery systems [2]. In many regions, health facilities operate within complex organizational environments that require coordinated decision-making between health professionals, local governments, community organizations, and policymakers [3]. However, governance processes often remain hierarchical and sectorally fragmented, limiting primary healthcare systems' ability to respond adaptively to population health needs [4]. 

The governance capacity of health systems has become increasingly important following the growing burden of chronic diseases, public health emergencies, and healthcare inequities [5]. Previous evidence has demonstrated that ineffective governance contributes to poor healthcare accessibility, inefficient resource allocation, low community trust, and suboptimal service integration [6]. Studies conducted in several developing countries have shown that leadership limitations within healthcare organizations frequently lead to delayed policy implementation, inconsistent health service standards, and weak institutional accountability [7]. In primary healthcare settings, leadership practices influence not only administrative performance but also interdisciplinary collaboration, workforce motivation, and community participation. Consequently, strengthening governance mechanisms has emerged as a strategic priority for improving healthcare system performance and sustainability [8]. 

Collaborative leadership has recently gained attention as an alternative governance approach capable of addressing organizational complexity in healthcare systems [9]. Unlike conventional hierarchical leadership models, collaborative leadership emphasizes shared decision-making, collective responsibility, stakeholder engagement, and cross-sectoral cooperation [10]. This leadership approach encourages healthcare managers, practitioners, local authorities, and community representatives to jointly participate in policy formulation and problem-solving in healthcare [11]. Existing studies have indicated that collaborative leadership may improve organizational adaptability, strengthen communication among healthcare actors, and support integrated service delivery [12]. Evidence from hospital and public health management research suggests that collaborative governance models are associated with improved institutional trust, greater innovation capacity, and stronger organizational resilience [13]. 

Several empirical studies have also highlighted the relationship between collaborative leadership and healthcare effectiveness.

Title: Strengthening health system governance through collaborative leadership to improve primary healthcare effectiveness
Snippet: Collaborative leadership may reduce these barriers by facilitating interprofessional interaction and promoting collective problem-solving among healthcare personnel [27]. Through collaborative governance processes, healthcare institutions may become more adaptive to local health priorities and more capable of responding efficiently to community healthcare needs [28]. 

The findings of this study are generally consistent with previous research emphasizing the importance of collaborative governance within healthcare organizations. Several earlier studies reported that participatory leadership approaches improved workforce engagement, institutional trust, and healthcare coordination [29]. Research conducted in community health programs and public health institutions also demonstrated that collaborative leadership strengthened policy implementation and enhanced organizational resilience during periods of healthcare uncertainty. Similar findings have been observed in studies examining integrated healthcare systems, where leadership collaboration was associated with improved communication and more efficient resource management. 

However, the present study extends previous literature in several important ways. First, much of the earlier research focused predominantly on hospital administration or organizational culture, while limited empirical evidence has examined collaborative leadership specifically within primary healthcare governance systems. Primary healthcare settings differ substantially from tertiary healthcare institutions because they operate closer to community populations and often face greater resource limitations, workforce shortages, and administrative fragmentation. By focusing on primary healthcare governance, this study contributes a more contextually relevant understanding of how collaborative leadership operates within frontline healthcare systems. 

Second, this study highlights the interconnectedness of leadership, governance, and healthcare effectiveness in decentralized healthcare environments. Existing literature frequently treats leadership competencies and governance quality as separate organizational constructs, whereas present findings demonstrate that these dimensions are structurally interconnected. Collaborative leadership may strengthen governance processes by improving stakeholder coordination, enhancing institutional participation, and promoting collective accountability. Consequently, healthcare effectiveness should not be interpreted solely as an operational outcome, but also as a reflection of governance quality and institutional collaboration. 

The study additionally contributes to broader conceptual discussions regarding health system governance in developing countries. Many healthcare reforms in low-and middle-income countries continue to emphasize administrative restructuring and financing expansion while paying relatively limited attention to collaborative governance processes. The findings suggest that governance effectiveness may depend not only on policy design or organizational resources but also on the quality of leadership interaction and institutional cooperation within healthcare systems. Strengthening collaborative leadership capacities may therefore represent a practical strategy for improving healthcare system resilience, particularly in settings characterized by limited resources and complex administrative arrangements. 

Despite these contributions, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.

Title: FROM POLICY TO PRACTICE: STRENGTHENING HEALTH SYSTEMS THROUGH EVIDENCE, EQUITY, AND INNOVATION
Snippet: Health systems worldwide are confronting increasingly complex challenges driven by demographic and epidemiological shifts transitions, technological advance, emerging health threats. Achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) therefore requires health systems that are not only accessible but also resilient, evidence-informed, and people-centered. This editorial synthesizes the contributions of the studies published in this issue through four interconnected dimensions of health system strengthening: governance and policy, service delivery and quality, the health workforce, and equity and innovation. The articles demonstrate that effective governance depends on translating evidence into coherent policies and successful implementation across different levels of the health system. High-quality service delivery requires organizational readiness, patient-centered care, and continuous quality improvement, while a resilient health workforce relies on supportive leadership, workforce well-being, and enabling work environments. The studies further highlight the importance of addressing social and geographic inequities and ensuring that technological innovations are implemented equitably to improve health outcomes across diverse populations. Together, these contributions reinforce the need for integrated, multisectoral, and evidence-informed strategies that connect governance, service delivery, workforce development, and equitable innovation. Strengthening these interconnected components is essential for building resilient health systems capable of responding to current challenges. 
Keyword: health systems, Universal Health Coverage, health policy.

Title: Sustainable Healthcare Models in Developing Countries: Bridging Gaps in Universal Health Coverage
Snippet: This distinction refines existing debates by emphasizing governance quality rather than structural form alone. 

The results signify that healthcare sustainability functions as an early indicator of longterm Universal Health Coverage success. Systems that prioritize sustainability demonstrate resilience against economic shocks, demographic changes, and public health crises. These characteristics reflect structural maturity within healthcare systems. The persistence of inequities in systems lacking sustainability signals deeper institutional and political challenges. Weak governance, fragmented policies, and unstable financing represent structural vulnerabilities rather than technical shortcomings. The findings thus point to sustainability as a marker of institutional strength (Chen et al., 2025;Iamtrakul et al., 2025). The case study outcomes indicate that sustainable healthcare models reflect deliberate policy choices rather than accidental success. Political commitment, strategic planning, and societal consensus emerge as underlying signals of system coherence. These elements distinguish transformative reforms from symbolic policy adoption. 

The findings imply that policy efforts focused solely on expanding coverage indicators are insufficient to achieve meaningful Universal Health Coverage. Sustainable financing and governance integration must accompany service expansion to ensure durability. Policymakers should reconsider reform strategies that prioritize scale over stability. Implications for health system planning include the need to rebalance investments toward primary and preventive care. Resource allocation patterns that favor curative services undermine long-term efficiency and financial sustainability. Strategic investment in early intervention can reduce systemic costs and inequities (Fedoriw et al., 2025;Iamtrakul et al., 2025). The study also implies broader development consequences beyond the health sector. Sustainable healthcare systems contribute to social stability, economic productivity, and poverty reduction. These implications position healthcare sustainability as a foundational component of national development strategies. 

The observed outcomes can be explained by the interdependent nature of health system components. Financing stability enables workforce retention, infrastructure maintenance, and service continuity. Disruptions in one component cascade across the system, weakening overall performance. Governance effectiveness explains variations in how policies translate into practice. Transparent institutions facilitate efficient resource allocation and accountability. Weak governance structures allow inefficiencies and inequities to persist despite formal policy commitments. Sociopolitical context also explains why sustainability differs across countries.

Title: Sustainable Healthcare Models in Developing Countries: Bridging Gaps in Universal Health Coverage

snippet.text:
Primary healthcare remains the cornerstone of equitable health systems and universal health coverage in many countries, particularly in low-and middle-income settings where healthcare resources are unevenly distributed [1]. Despite ongoing reforms in healthcare administration and financing, the effectiveness of primary healthcare services continues to be hampered by major governance challenges. Weak institutional coordination, fragmented leadership structures, limited accountability mechanisms, and inadequate collaboration among stakeholders frequently reduce the responsiveness and efficiency of healthcare delivery systems [2]. In many regions, health facilities operate within complex organizational environments that require coordinated decision-making between health professionals, local governments, community organizations, and policymakers [3]. However, governance processes often remain hierarchical and sectorally fragmented, limiting primary healthcare systems' ability to respond adaptively to population health needs [4]. 

The governance capacity of health systems has become increasingly important following the growing burden of chronic diseases, public health emergencies, and healthcare inequities [5]. Previous evidence has demonstrated that ineffective governance contributes to poor healthcare accessibility, inefficient resource allocation, low community trust, and suboptimal service integration [6]. Studies conducted in several developing countries have shown that leadership limitations within healthcare organizations frequently lead to delayed policy implementation, inconsistent health service standards, and weak institutional accountability [7]. In primary healthcare settings, leadership practices influence not only administrative performance but also interdisciplinary collaboration, workforce motivation, and community participation. Consequently, strengthening governance mechanisms has emerged as a strategic priority for improving healthcare system performance and sustainability [8]. 

Collaborative leadership has recently gained attention as an alternative governance approach capable of addressing organizational complexity in healthcare systems [9]. Unlike conventional hierarchical leadership models, collaborative leadership emphasizes shared decision-making, collective responsibility, stakeholder engagement, and cross-sectoral cooperation [10]. This leadership approach encourages healthcare managers, practitioners, local authorities, and community representatives to jointly participate in policy formulation and problem-solving in healthcare [11]. Existing studies have indicated that collaborative leadership may improve organizational adaptability, strengthen communication among healthcare actors, and support integrated service delivery [12]. Evidence from hospital and public health management research suggests that collaborative governance models are associated with improved institutional trust, greater innovation capacity, and stronger organizational resilience [13]. 

Several empirical studies have also highlighted the relationship between collaborative leadership and healthcare effectiveness.

Through collaborative governance processes, healthcare institutions may become more adaptive to local health priorities and more capable of responding efficiently to community healthcare needs [28]. 

The findings of this study are generally consistent with previous research emphasizing the importance of collaborative governance within healthcare organizations. Several earlier studies reported that participatory leadership approaches improved workforce engagement, institutional trust, and healthcare coordination [29]. Research conducted in community health programs and public health institutions also demonstrated that collaborative leadership strengthened policy implementation and enhanced organizational resilience during periods of healthcare uncertainty. Similar findings have been observed in studies examining integrated healthcare systems, where leadership collaboration was associated with improved communication and more efficient resource management. 

However, the present study extends previous literature in several important ways. First, much of the earlier research focused predominantly on hospital administration or organizational culture, while limited empirical evidence has examined collaborative leadership specifically within primary healthcare governance systems. Primary healthcare settings differ substantially from tertiary healthcare institutions because they operate closer to community populations and often face greater resource limitations, workforce shortages, and administrative fragmentation. By focusing on primary healthcare governance, this study contributes a more contextually relevant understanding of how collaborative leadership operates within frontline healthcare systems. 

Second, this study highlights the interconnectedness of leadership, governance, and healthcare effectiveness in decentralized healthcare environments. Existing literature frequently treats leadership competencies and governance quality as separate organizational constructs, whereas present findings demonstrate that these dimensions are structurally interconnected. Collaborative leadership may strengthen governance processes by improving stakeholder coordination, enhancing institutional participation, and promoting collective accountability. Consequently, healthcare effectiveness should not be interpreted solely as an operational outcome, but also as a reflection of governance quality and institutional collaboration. 

The study additionally contributes to broader conceptual discussions regarding health system governance in developing countries. Many healthcare reforms in low-and middle-income countries continue to emphasize administrative restructuring and financing expansion while paying relatively limited attention to collaborative governance processes. The findings suggest that governance effectiveness may depend not only on policy design or organizational resources but also on the quality of leadership interaction and institutional cooperation within healthcare systems. Strengthening collaborative leadership capacities may therefore represent a practical strategy for improving healthcare system resilience, particularly in settings characterized by limited resources and complex administrative arrangements. 

Despite these contributions, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.

snippet.text:
Health systems worldwide are confronting increasingly complex challenges driven by demographic and epidemiological shifts transitions, technological advance, emerging health threats. Achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) therefore requires health systems that are not only accessible but also resilient, evidence-informed, and people-centered. This editorial synthesizes the contributions of the studies published in this issue through four interconnected dimensions of health system strengthening: governance and policy, service delivery and quality, the health workforce, and equity and innovation. The articles demonstrate that effective governance depends on translating evidence into coherent policies and successful implementation across different levels of the health system. High-quality service delivery requires organizational readiness, patient-centered care, and continuous quality improvement, while a resilient health workforce relies on supportive leadership, workforce well-being, and enabling work environments. The studies further highlight the importance of addressing social and geographic inequities and ensuring that technological innovations are implemented equitably to improve health outcomes across diverse populations. Together, these contributions reinforce the need for integrated, multisectoral, and evidence-informed strategies that connect governance, service delivery, workforce development, and equitable innovation. Strengthening these interconnected components is essential for building resilient health systems capable of responding to current challenges. 
Keyword: health systems, Universal Health Coverage, health policy.

This distinction refines existing debates by emphasizing governance quality rather than structural form alone. 

The results signify that healthcare sustainability functions as an early indicator of longterm Universal Health Coverage success. Systems that prioritize sustainability demonstrate resilience against economic shocks, demographic changes, and public health crises. These characteristics reflect structural maturity within healthcare systems. The persistence of inequities in systems lacking sustainability signals deeper institutional and political challenges. Weak governance, fragmented policies, and unstable financing represent structural vulnerabilities rather than technical shortcomings. The findings thus point to sustainability as a marker of institutional strength (Chen et al., 2025;Iamtrakul et al., 2025). The case study outcomes indicate that sustainable healthcare models reflect deliberate policy choices rather than accidental success. Political commitment, strategic planning, and societal consensus emerge as underlying signals of system coherence. These elements distinguish transformative reforms from symbolic policy adoption. 

The findings imply that policy efforts focused solely on expanding coverage indicators are insufficient to achieve meaningful Universal Health Coverage. Sustainable financing and governance integration must accompany service expansion to ensure durability. Policymakers should reconsider reform strategies that prioritize scale over stability. Implications for health system planning include the need to rebalance investments toward primary and preventive care. Resource allocation patterns that favor curative services undermine long-term efficiency and financial sustainability. Strategic investment in early intervention can reduce systemic costs and inequities (Fedoriw et al., 2025;Iamtrakul et al., 2025). The study also implies broader development consequences beyond the health sector. Sustainable healthcare systems contribute to social stability, economic productivity, and poverty reduction. These implications position healthcare sustainability as a foundational component of national development strategies. 

The observed outcomes can be explained by the interdependent nature of health system components. Financing stability enables workforce retention, infrastructure maintenance, and service continuity. Disruptions in one component cascade across the system, weakening overall performance. Governance effectiveness explains variations in how policies translate into practice. Transparent institutions facilitate efficient resource allocation and accountability. Weak governance structures allow inefficiencies and inequities to persist despite formal policy commitments. Sociopolitical context also explains why sustainability differs across countries.

attempts.answer:
Overview and framing

Transformative sustainability in healthcare means innovations that shift systems toward better population health, equitable access, and lower environmental footprint at scale. Realizing such impact is obstructed by barriers that differ for emerging versus established innovations because early-stage solutions face adoption and legitimacy hurdles in complex organizations, while entrenched solutions struggle with locked-in incentives, fragmented governance, and legacy infrastructure that dampen system-wide change. Leadership and governance must therefore tailor capabilities: cultivate cross-sector alignment and participatory legitimacy for emerging innovations, and reconfigure incentives, mandates, and accreditation for entrenched systems to drive durable change. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Struggle to juggle strategic responsibilities with daily operations, time/resource constraints, and rigid hierarchical decision-making are systemic barriers that stifle innovation and adaptability</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Transformational and authentic leadership and robust governance frameworks drive cultural and structural change, but evidence on causal pathways remains fragmented</cite>.

Barriers unique to emerging, disruptive innovations

Emerging innovations often begin with promise but face adoption and scale-up barriers rooted in organizational complexity and risk-averse regimes. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Misalignment between administrative priorities and the adaptive changes required for practical innovation, limited financial and infrastructure resources, and resistance to change that fears added workload are common barriers</cite>. Participatory, co-designed approaches can address legitimacy and workflow fit, yet demand leadership that actively champions change and aligns incentives across clinical, administrative, and community stakeholders. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Involving administrative leaders early to align innovation priorities, privileging low-cost/high-impact solutions to reduce resource barriers, and cultivating a cultural shift via leadership participation can counter resistance and streamline workflow</cite>. Workforce-driven innovation shows that knowledge deficits, poor leadership, weak inter- and cross-organizational learning, inadequate communication networks, and structural barriers impede progress; these are salient for early-stage technologies that rely on clinician engagement and local adaptation. <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Major impediments include lack of knowledge/resources and financial constraints, poor leadership, limited inter- and cross-organizational learning, structural communication barriers, and resistance to change</cite>.

Two further barriers are distinctive for emerging digital/social innovations. First, participatory governance for justice and trust: innovations that alter care delivery models or data flows need community engagement and cross-sector alignment to secure “social license” and ensure equitable benefits. <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Governance and policy bridge micro-level actions to macro-level impact, requiring engagement at management and policy levels to integrate innovations into broader strategies and address societal concerns</cite>. Second, data and interoperability gaps limit measurement and diffusion. Without shared platforms and governance arrangements to validate and disseminate results, promising pilots stall before scale. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Collaborative development and distribution through innovators and early adopters improves contextual alignment and local relevance, facilitating sustainable diffusion</cite>.

Barriers unique to established, entrenched innovations

Established innovations face barriers of inertia and fragmented governance as systems scale down, not up: unclear institutional mandates, policy fragmentation, and finance constraints for retrofitting legacy infrastructure and supply chains. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Absence of decarbonization targets and regulatory support, unclear institutional mandates, and fragmented policies across health and environmental agencies create confusion, gaps in enforcement, and limit accountability for environmental outcomes</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Financial barriers include insufficient collateral, lack of credit history, and limited familiarity with climate finance; hospitals with weaker institutional support face steeper hurdles than developed settings with dedicated sustainability funding</cite>. Operational complexity is magnified by supply chains: emissions concentrated in procurement and energy make “business-as-usual” accounting and incentives blind to systemwide footprints. <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Supply chain activities account for over 80% of total emissions; aligning sustainability leadership, incentives, and emissions tracking with national NDC targets is essential to drive sectoral progress</cite>.

Equity and community impact also become harder to retrofit into mature services. Without explicit governance to redirect payment and contracting toward social outcomes and environmental stewardship, established programs externalize costs onto communities and the climate while improving narrow clinical metrics. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Integrating sustainability objectives into organizational governance, strategic planning, and performance management, and strengthening leadership engagement and sustainability management capability, are associated with stronger social sustainability practices</cite>. <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Policy innovation must extend beyond health outcomes to encompass environmental and social considerations, balancing patient care with climate and equity concerns</cite>.

How leadership and governance differ by innovation stage

For emerging innovations: leadership must be “boundary spanning” and participatory to secure adoption and scale. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Engaging administrative leaders early aligns organizational goals and reduces misalignment between policy and adaptive change</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Protected time for strategic planning, leadership training and development, and redefining leadership effectiveness to include innovation and culture metrics can counter time/resource and hierarchical barriers</cite>. Governance should enable experimentation and knowledge sharing: <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">collaborative development and distribution through innovators and early adopters improves contextual fit and accelerates diffusion</cite>, and <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">clarifying goals, granting resource autonomy, and navigating regulatory changes through stakeholder engagement at management and policy levels</cite>.

Financial and data levers are critical: <cite id="b80c36b8-1">investment in operational sustainability and digital healthcare transformation improves efficiency, adaptability, and accessibility, and should be embedded in governance and performance systems</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Accreditation and certification that tie sustainability progress to reaccreditation, combined with public emissions reporting and supply-chain inventories, can catalyze action for both emerging and entrenched innovations</cite>.

For established innovations: governance must mandate and institutionalize sustainability as a system operating objective. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Established targets, coordinated low‑carbon roadmaps, and clear assignment of responsibilities across agencies are needed to overcome fragmented policy and unclear mandates</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Sustainability leadership, incentive structures tied to emissions reductions, sustainable procurement, and alignment with national climate targets create durable accountability and drive supply-chain transformation</cite>. For workforce and operations, governance should codify continuous improvement into compliance and accreditation cycles and strengthen inter-organizational learning to avoid repeating local failures at scale. <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Improving communication networks, leadership quality, and inter-organizational learning addresses persistent barriers to workforce-driven innovation</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Clinical and overall governance strengthen accountability, transparency, and risk management, sustaining performance improvements when leadership and governance act synergistically</cite>.

Environmental sustainability: contrasting constraints and levers

Emerging innovations can achieve faster relative change by leveraging digital transformation, co-design, and new payment/contract models that value externalities, but they often lack the institutional heft to change system-wide baselines. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Digital healthcare systems improve efficiency and adaptability and can be leveraged to embed sustainability objectives in governance and performance</cite>. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Low-cost, high-impact designs and participatory implementation reduce resource barriers and promote more equitable innovation</cite>. Established systems face steeper structural barriers to decarbonization and system transformation: finance frictions, fragmented mandates, and supply-chain lock-in. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Hospitals in developing contexts face green finance barriers (collateral, credit history, unfamiliarity with climate finance) and fragmented policy/regulatory environments, requiring tailored credit facilities, guarantees, and public–private partnerships</cite> <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Absence of targets and unclear institutional mandates stall progress, demanding coordinated policy frameworks and integrated governance</cite>. Governance responses must therefore combine sector-wide targets, procurement power, and accreditation to shift established operations: <cite id="e6d678a4-1">annual emissions data aggregation and public reporting, targets, supply-chain decarbonization via purchasing power, and tying carbon performance to incentives and accreditation can institutionalize accountability</cite>.

Equity-centered governance and leadership

Both stages require equity-centered leadership, but the institutional anchors differ. Emerging innovations need leaders who can broker community trust and align pilots with social needs; established systems need leaders who can re-align budgets and contracts to distribute benefits and burdens fairly. <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Governance and policy must address societal concerns and bridge micro-to-macro impact through stakeholder engagement</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Organizational readiness, governance coordination, and executive commitment are essential for embedding sustainability; digital transformation can improve accessibility and efficiency</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Leadership effectiveness should be measured with qualitative indicators of culture, innovation, and wellbeing, and protected time and training can build resilient, adaptive systems</cite>.

Practical playbook: matching barriers to mechanisms

- Co-create and pilot with frontline teams and communities to overcome adoption and workflow-fit barriers for emerging innovations; embed results into digital platforms and improvement cycles to accelerate diffusion. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Participatory design, leadership alignment, and low-cost/high-impact solutions counter misalignment, resource constraints, and resistance</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Digital systems and ESG integration provide operational and governance scaffolding</cite>.
- For entrenched systems, set explicit decarbonization targets, integrate sustainability into accreditation and budgeting, and leverage procurement and supply-chain contracts to drive sectoral impact. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Coordinated policy roadmaps and clear mandates overcome fragmented governance</cite> <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Incentive alignment, emissions tracking, and public reporting institutionalize accountability</cite>.
- Strengthen leadership capacity for change: protected strategic time, development of innovation-capable leaders, and measurement that includes culture and equity. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Protected time, training, and redefined metrics enable proactive leadership amid operational pressures</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Transformational/authentic leadership and clinical governance provide synergistic structural support</cite>.
- Build inter-organizational learning networks and communication infrastructures to spread best practices and avoid scale-ups of local failures. <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Improved communication networks, leadership quality, and inter-organizational learning mitigate workforce-driven innovation barriers</cite>.

Synthesis and implications

Emerging innovations are uniquely hindered by organizational ambivalence, workforce engagement gaps, and finance/data frictions that slow diffusion and legitimacy, while established innovations are obstructed by fragmented mandates, supply-chain lock-in, and finance barriers that dampen system-wide decarbonization and equity improvements. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Administrative misalignment, resource limits, and resistance to change require participatory alignment and low-cost, workflow-friendly designs</cite> <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Workforce-driven barriers demand learning networks and leadership improvements</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">For entrenched systems, lack of targets, unclear mandates, and fragmented policies must be replaced with coordinated roadmaps and financing mechanisms</cite> <cite id="e6d678a4-1">and sustainability must be embedded in incentives, procurement, and accreditation</cite>. Leadership and governance mechanisms therefore differ by stage: early-stage solutions need boundary-spanning leaders and participatory governance to secure adoption and diffusion, while mature systems need mandate-setting, incentive realignment, and accreditation-driven accountability to achieve durable, transformative sustainability at scale. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Embedding sustainability into governance, strategic planning, and performance management, with investment in digital transformation and leadership capability, supports long-term social sustainability</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Transformational leadership paired with clinical governance strengthens accountability and cultural change</cite> <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Governance structures that engage stakeholders from management to policy levels bridge micro-to-macro impact and integrate environmental and social concerns</cite>.

Open gaps and next steps

Evidence on causal pathways linking leadership styles to sustainability outcomes across contexts remains fragmented, and comparative analyses explicitly separating “emerging” vs “established” barriers are limited. <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Empirical evidence is fragmented regarding causal pathways and mediating factors</cite>. Future work should longitudinal, multi-site studies that track how participatory governance and accreditation-incentive systems change adoption, equity, and emissions outcomes across innovation maturity, and evaluate the role of community engagement in securing social license for digital and data-driven innovations. <cite id="e0f48cc3-3">Understanding relationships among organizational culture, finance, and sustainability is essential, particularly for interventions that foster cultures of sustainable innovation</cite>.

Title: The Actionable Innovation Day Approach: Participatory Model for Advancing Critical Care Innovation
Snippet: Systemic barriers often impede health care innovation [11]. The AID approach deliberately addressed these barriers by incorporating specific strategies designed to facilitate a conducive environment to implement change. One significant barrier to health care innovation is the misalignment between administrative priorities and the adaptive, rapid changes required for practical innovation [11]. Policymakers and administrators may be reluctant to embrace such changes due to concerns about potential risks, costs, or disruptions to established processes. The AID event actively involved administrative leaders throughout the event to align innovation priorities with organizational goals, enabling smoother adoption and increasing the likelihood of long-term integration. Furthermore, the intention to promote incremental innovation, as opposed to radical invention, ensures that the implementation process can be more readily navigated. A second substantial barrier involves the limited availability of financial and infrastructure resources [7]. High-cost innovations can be particularly challenging to implement in resource-constrained environments such as Canadian health care. The AID framework addressed this challenge by emphasizing low-cost, high-impact solutions that required minimal resource investment. This approach not only made the proposed innovations more feasible for a wide range of institutions but also reduced barriers related to resource allocation, thereby promoting more equitable innovation. Third, the diffusion of innovation is another critical aspect of sustainable health care change [12,13]. The AID approach promoted the diffusion of recommendations in several ways. The recommendations are naturally distributed throughout the health authority by involving innovators and early adopters across most disciplines and from sites across the region. Similarly, because of the collaborative approach to developing the recommendations, those involved are more likely to appreciate the relevance and alignment of the proposed solutions to the specific context of their local community. Finally, by inviting administrators, we hope to promote a cultural shift that promotes innovation from those in leadership roles. Leaders who actively participate in and advocate for innovative initiatives set a positive example, foster a supportive culture, and help embed innovation as an organizational value [14]. Barriers such as resistance to change often hinder the adoption of new practices. This resistance can be exacerbated by fears that new innovations will add to the workload of already overburdened health care teams. The AID framework sought to counter these concerns by focusing on innovations designed to streamline workflows and reduce unnecessary burdens.

Title: Barriers to Workforce-Driven Innovation in Healthcare

Title: Decarbonizing Indonesian hospitals challenges and causal pathways toward sustainable healthcare
Snippet: In Banten, a similar pattern was observed, where local hospitals faced challenges in securing green loans or investment due to insufficient collateral, lack of credit history, and limited familiarity with climate finance mechanisms. 's cases in developed countries, where hospitals may have established financial management systems and access to dedicated sustainability funding, Banten hospitals are constrained by weaker institutional support and less experience in low-carbon project financing. Unclear institutional mandates mean that responsibilities for implementing low-carbon initiatives are not well defined, causing confusion among hospital staff and limiting accountability for environmental outcomes. Given this situation, the case of Banten exemplifies the need for coordinated policy frameworks and integrated governance structures. This underscores the need for the Provincial Health Office and Environmental Agency to formulate integrated low-carbon healthcare roadmaps and include hospitals within the Regional Action Plan for Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction (RAD-GRK), ensuring clear assignment of responsibilities and alignment of policies across institutional levels.

Title: Bridging health and global climate policy: Opportunities for policymakers and health systems
Snippet: Health systems leaders can advance decarbonization by aggregating and analyzing emissions data annually, setting emissions targets, reducing energy use and waste, and publicly reporting on progress for their own environmental footprint [28]. Institutional mechanisms should include sustainability leadership, incentive structures tied to sustainability progress [29], and alignment with national NDC targets to ensure transparency and enable sectoral progress tracking. Since supply chain activities account for over 80 % of total emissions, transitioning to sustainable procurement and operations is essential [30,29]. By integrating sustainability criteria into purchasing decisions, the healthcare sector can leverage their significant market power to influence suppliers to adopt lower-emission practices. In doing so, the healthcare sector can set a benchmark for adjacent industries like manufacturing, transportation, and energy to follow [31]. Insurance can further accelerate this shift by incentivizing low-emission practices and climate-conscious programs, as Medicare and Medicaid have already begun piloting in the US [32]. 

Several countries offer lessons for decarbonization strategies. In the United States (U.S.), more than 1200 hospitalsrepresenting over 19 % of U.S. hospitalshave signed the Health Sector Climate Pledge, committing to reducing emissions 50 % by 2030 and achieving net zero emissions by 2050 [33]. These institutions pledge to publish annual progress, conduct supply chain emissions inventories, and develop resilience plans for vulnerable communities. In the United Kingdom (U. K.), the National Health Service (NHS) has committed to becoming the world's first net-zero health system, supported by emissions tracking, green procurement policies, and carbon literacy training for clinical staff. 

Accreditation bodies can play a critical role in scaling health sector decarbonization. In the U.S., the Joint Commission has launched a sustainability certification program that provides resources to support hospitals in transitioning to more sustainable operations. To ensure lasting impact, decarbonization progress should be incorporated into the Joint Commission's reaccreditation process. In the U.K., the NHS has tied carbon performance to financial and operational incentives. Title: Decarbonizing Indonesian hospitals challenges and causal pathways toward sustainable healthcare
Snippet: A comprehensive literature review was conducted to identify potential barriers to hospital decarbonizing based on previous studies in healthcare sustainability, green hospital implementation, and environmental management in emerging economies. Specifically, the literature search was performed using databases such as Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, with keywords including "hospital decarbonization, " "healthcare sustainability, " "green hospital, " "environmental management, " and "emerging economies. " This preliminary list was further refined through consultations with academic experts, hospital administrators, and environmental management professionals in Indonesia. The final list of barriers was categorized into key thematic groups, including financial, technical, regulatory, organizational, and socio-cultural aspects (see Table 2).
</snippet></tool_output> 
<think>
Sufficiency check: We have evidence on (1) leadership/governance barriers (time/resources, rigid hierarchies, misaligned incentives), (2) mechanisms that help early-stage and system-level sustainability (participatory innovation, alignment with policy, digital transformation, ESG integration), and (3) environmental decarbonization barriers and levers specific to established systems (finance, fragmented policy, unclear mandates, supply chains), including concrete governance tools (targets, reporting, accreditation, procurement). We also have evidence on workforce-driven innovation barriers and the importance of leadership, inter-organizational learning, and culture, which helps differentiate mechanisms for emerging vs established innovations. Remaining gaps include highly detailed comparative frameworks explicitly mapping “barriers unique to emerging” versus “established,” and more on community governance/social license for digital/transformative innovations; however, current snippets cover the core contrasts and mechanisms needed for an evidence-backed synthesis. I will structure the answer with: (1) framing, (2) barriers by innovation stage, (3) differences in governance and leadership by stage, (4) environmental sustainability contrasts, and (5) practical playbook and gaps.
</think>
<answer>
Overview and framing

Transformative sustainability in healthcare means innovations that shift systems toward better population health, equitable access, and lower environmental footprint at scale. Realizing such impact is obstructed by barriers that differ for emerging versus established innovations because early-stage solutions face adoption and legitimacy hurdles in complex organizations, while entrenched solutions struggle with locked-in incentives, fragmented governance, and legacy infrastructure that dampen system-wide change. Leadership and governance must therefore tailor capabilities: cultivate cross-sector alignment and participatory legitimacy for emerging innovations, and reconfigure incentives, mandates, and accreditation for entrenched systems to drive durable change. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Struggle to juggle strategic responsibilities with daily operations, time/resource constraints, and rigid hierarchical decision-making are systemic barriers that stifle innovation and adaptability</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Transformational and authentic leadership and robust governance frameworks drive cultural and structural change, but evidence on causal pathways remains fragmented</cite>.

Barriers unique to emerging, disruptive innovations

Emerging innovations often begin with promise but face adoption and scale-up barriers rooted in organizational complexity and risk-averse regimes. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Misalignment between administrative priorities and the adaptive changes required for practical innovation, limited financial and infrastructure resources, and resistance to change that fears added workload are common barriers</cite>. Participatory, co-designed approaches can address legitimacy and workflow fit, yet demand leadership that actively champions change and aligns incentives across clinical, administrative, and community stakeholders. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Involving administrative leaders early to align innovation priorities, privileging low-cost/high-impact solutions to reduce resource barriers, and cultivating a cultural shift via leadership participation can counter resistance and streamline workflow</cite>. Workforce-driven innovation shows that knowledge deficits, poor leadership, weak inter- and cross-organizational learning, inadequate communication networks, and structural barriers impede progress; these are salient for early-stage technologies that rely on clinician engagement and local adaptation. <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Major impediments include lack of knowledge/resources and financial constraints, poor leadership, limited inter- and cross-organizational learning, structural communication barriers, and resistance to change</cite>.

Two further barriers are distinctive for emerging digital/social innovations. First, participatory governance for justice and trust: innovations that alter care delivery models or data flows need community engagement and cross-sector alignment to secure “social license” and ensure equitable benefits. <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Governance and policy bridge micro-level actions to macro-level impact, requiring engagement at management and policy levels to integrate innovations into broader strategies and address societal concerns</cite>. Second, data and interoperability gaps limit measurement and diffusion. Without shared platforms and governance arrangements to validate and disseminate results, promising pilots stall before scale. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Collaborative development and distribution through innovators and early adopters improves contextual alignment and local relevance, facilitating sustainable diffusion</cite>.

Barriers unique to established, entrenched innovations

Established innovations face barriers of inertia and fragmented governance as systems scale down, not up: unclear institutional mandates, policy fragmentation, and finance constraints for retrofitting legacy infrastructure and supply chains. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Absence of decarbonization targets and regulatory support, unclear institutional mandates, and fragmented policies across health and environmental agencies create confusion, gaps in enforcement, and limit accountability for environmental outcomes</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Financial barriers include insufficient collateral, lack of credit history, and limited familiarity with climate finance; hospitals with weaker institutional support face steeper hurdles than developed settings with dedicated sustainability funding</cite>. Operational complexity is magnified by supply chains: emissions concentrated in procurement and energy make “business-as-usual” accounting and incentives blind to systemwide footprints. <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Supply chain activities account for over 80% of total emissions; aligning sustainability leadership, incentives, and emissions tracking with national NDC targets is essential to drive sectoral progress</cite>.

Equity and community impact also become harder to retrofit into mature services. Without explicit governance to redirect payment and contracting toward social outcomes and environmental stewardship, established programs externalize costs onto communities and the climate while improving narrow clinical metrics. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Integrating sustainability objectives into organizational governance, strategic planning, and performance management, and strengthening leadership engagement and sustainability management capability, are associated with stronger social sustainability practices</cite>. <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Policy innovation must extend beyond health outcomes to encompass environmental and social considerations, balancing patient care with climate and equity concerns</cite>.

How leadership and governance differ by innovation stage

For emerging innovations: leadership must be “boundary spanning” and participatory to secure adoption and scale. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Engaging administrative leaders early aligns organizational goals and reduces misalignment between policy and adaptive change</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Protected time for strategic planning, leadership training and development, and redefining leadership effectiveness to include innovation and culture metrics can counter time/resource and hierarchical barriers</cite>. Governance should enable experimentation and knowledge sharing: <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">collaborative development and distribution through innovators and early adopters improves contextual fit and accelerates diffusion</cite>, and <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">clarifying goals, granting resource autonomy, and navigating regulatory changes through stakeholder engagement at management and policy levels</cite>.

Financial and data levers are critical: <cite id="b80c36b8-1">investment in operational sustainability and digital healthcare transformation improves efficiency, adaptability, and accessibility, and should be embedded in governance and performance systems</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Accreditation and certification that tie sustainability progress to reaccreditation, combined with public emissions reporting and supply-chain inventories, can catalyze action for both emerging and entrenched innovations</cite>.

For established innovations: governance must mandate and institutionalize sustainability as a system operating objective. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Established targets, coordinated low‑carbon roadmaps, and clear assignment of responsibilities across agencies are needed to overcome fragmented policy and unclear mandates</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Sustainability leadership, incentive structures tied to emissions reductions, sustainable procurement, and alignment with national climate targets create durable accountability and drive supply-chain transformation</cite>. For workforce and operations, governance should codify continuous improvement into compliance and accreditation cycles and strengthen inter-organizational learning to avoid repeating local failures at scale. <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Improving communication networks, leadership quality, and inter-organizational learning addresses persistent barriers to workforce-driven innovation</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Clinical and overall governance strengthen accountability, transparency, and risk management, sustaining performance improvements when leadership and governance act synergistically</cite>.

Environmental sustainability: contrasting constraints and levers

Emerging innovations can achieve faster relative change by leveraging digital transformation, co-design, and new payment/contract models that value externalities, but they often lack the institutional heft to change system-wide baselines. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Digital healthcare systems improve efficiency and adaptability and can be leveraged to embed sustainability objectives in governance and performance</cite>. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Low-cost, high-impact designs and participatory implementation reduce resource barriers and promote more equitable innovation</cite>. Established systems face steeper structural barriers to decarbonization and system transformation: finance frictions, fragmented mandates, and supply-chain lock-in. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Hospitals in developing contexts face green finance barriers (collateral, credit history, unfamiliarity with climate finance) and fragmented policy/regulatory environments, requiring tailored credit facilities, guarantees, and public–private partnerships</cite> <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Absence of targets and unclear institutional mandates stall progress, demanding coordinated policy frameworks and integrated governance</cite>. Governance responses must therefore combine sector-wide targets, procurement power, and accreditation to shift established operations: <cite id="e6d678a4-1">annual emissions data aggregation and public reporting, targets, supply-chain decarbonization via purchasing power, and tying carbon performance to incentives and accreditation can institutionalize accountability</cite>.

Equity-centered governance and leadership

Both stages require equity-centered leadership, but the institutional anchors differ. Emerging innovations need leaders who can broker community trust and align pilots with social needs; established systems need leaders who can re-align budgets and contracts to distribute benefits and burdens fairly. <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Governance and policy must address societal concerns and bridge micro-to-macro impact through stakeholder engagement</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Organizational readiness, governance coordination, and executive commitment are essential for embedding sustainability; digital transformation can improve accessibility and efficiency</cite>. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Leadership effectiveness should be measured with qualitative indicators of culture, innovation, and wellbeing, and protected time and training can build resilient, adaptive systems</cite>.

Practical playbook: matching barriers to mechanisms

- Co-create and pilot with frontline teams and communities to overcome adoption and workflow-fit barriers for emerging innovations; embed results into digital platforms and improvement cycles to accelerate diffusion. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Participatory design, leadership alignment, and low-cost/high-impact solutions counter misalignment, resource constraints, and resistance</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Digital systems and ESG integration provide operational and governance scaffolding</cite>.
- For entrenched systems, set explicit decarbonization targets, integrate sustainability into accreditation and budgeting, and leverage procurement and supply-chain contracts to drive sectoral impact. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">Coordinated policy roadmaps and clear mandates overcome fragmented governance</cite> <cite id="e6d678a4-1">Incentive alignment, emissions tracking, and public reporting institutionalize accountability</cite>.
- Strengthen leadership capacity for change: protected strategic time, development of innovation-capable leaders, and measurement that includes culture and equity. <cite id="b80c36b8-0">Protected time, training, and redefined metrics enable proactive leadership amid operational pressures</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Transformational/authentic leadership and clinical governance provide synergistic structural support</cite>.
- Build inter-organizational learning networks and communication infrastructures to spread best practices and avoid scale-ups of local failures. <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Improved communication networks, leadership quality, and inter-organizational learning mitigate workforce-driven innovation barriers</cite>.

Synthesis and implications

Emerging innovations are uniquely hindered by organizational ambivalence, workforce engagement gaps, and finance/data frictions that slow diffusion and legitimacy, while established innovations are obstructed by fragmented mandates, supply-chain lock-in, and finance barriers that dampen system-wide decarbonization and equity improvements. <cite id="e0f48cc3-0">Administrative misalignment, resource limits, and resistance to change require participatory alignment and low-cost, workflow-friendly designs</cite> <cite id="e0f48cc3-2">Workforce-driven barriers demand learning networks and leadership improvements</cite>. <cite id="e6d678a4-0">For entrenched systems, lack of targets, unclear mandates, and fragmented policies must be replaced with coordinated roadmaps and financing mechanisms</cite> <cite id="e6d678a4-1">and sustainability must be embedded in incentives, procurement, and accreditation</cite>. Leadership and governance mechanisms therefore differ by stage: early-stage solutions need boundary-spanning leaders and participatory governance to secure adoption and diffusion, while mature systems need mandate-setting, incentive realignment, and accreditation-driven accountability to achieve durable, transformative sustainability at scale. <cite id="b80c36b8-1">Embedding sustainability into governance, strategic planning, and performance management, with investment in digital transformation and leadership capability, supports long-term social sustainability</cite> <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Transformational leadership paired with clinical governance strengthens accountability and cultural change</cite> <cite id="e0f48cc3-1">Governance structures that engage stakeholders from management to policy levels bridge micro-to-macro impact and integrate environmental and social concerns</cite>.

Open gaps and next steps

Evidence on causal pathways linking leadership styles to sustainability outcomes across contexts remains fragmented, and comparative analyses explicitly separating “emerging” vs “established” barriers are limited. <cite id="b80c36b8-2">Empirical evidence is fragmented regarding causal pathways and mediating factors</cite>. Future work should longitudinal, multi-site studies that track how participatory governance and accreditation-incentive systems change adoption, equity, and emissions outcomes across innovation maturity, and evaluate the role of community engagement in securing social license for digital and data-driven innovations. <cite id="e0f48cc3-3">Understanding relationships among organizational culture, finance, and sustainability is essential, particularly for interventions that foster cultures of sustainable innovation</cite>.
</answer>
